title: Feedback Notes: an Outcome the submitter is told about, set by the issue close and never written by hand
label: OPEN
body:
## Problem Statement

A user leaves a Feedback Note and never hears anything again.

The loop is half-built, and every arrow in it points inward. A Note is written to Firestore and an issue is opened from it. A Full-timer can move its status or archive it in the admin list. When the issue closes, a webhook writes `status: 'resolved'` back onto the Note, and a close as `not_planned` additionally archives it. At no point is the person who wrote the Note told anything. The submit page writes `userId` once and never reads it back: there is no view of your own Notes, no notification, no email. The Note's state changes in a database and no human learns of it.

So a Full-timer cannot assure anyone their Note was heard, cannot tell them it shipped, cannot tell them it is not planned, and — the case that prompted this — cannot tell them the thing they asked for already exists in the app. [#961](https://github.com/Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker/issues/961) is a user asking for a feature that is arguably already on a page he was standing on. Nothing in the system can say so.

The obvious fix — a reply box on the admin list — is the wrong one. It puts a writing task on a Full-timer for every Note, which means in practice it is used twice and then never again, and a response channel that works sometimes is worse than one that always works. The constraint is therefore firm: **no new authoring load**. Whatever reaches the submitter must be generated from an action the maintainer already takes.

## Solution

A Note gains an **Outcome** — what became of it, as its submitter would put it: it shipped, it is not planned, or it is already there. The Outcome is set automatically when the work behind the Note closes, and the submitter is told in one fixed sentence, called **What came of it**.

Two of the three Outcomes are already free. GitHub's `state_reason` on close distinguishes "completed" from "not planned", the Note already carries its issue URL, and the webhook already fires. Only "this already exists" has no signal in a close event, and it costs exactly one thing: an `already-exists` label applied at close, in the UI the maintainer is already in at the moment they are already there.

The submitter gets both a **place** and a **ping**. The place is a list of their own Notes under the composer on the feedback page, which everyone who can submit can already reach. The ping rides the existing notifications collection. The ping is the part that does the work — a page nobody visits assures nobody.

Two smaller corrections travel with this. "Not planned" stops being an archive and becomes a visible Outcome: it is the answer most worth explaining and it was the one disappearing fastest and quietest. And Outcome becomes a field of its own beside `status`, because `status` answers *where is this in our pipeline* and belongs to the team, while an Outcome answers *what became of my Note* and belongs to the person who wrote it.

Asking a submitter a question stays out of the app entirely — in person, by text, or in Messages. A Note remains a one-shot note, never a thread.

This is recorded as ADR 0017.

## User Stories

### Hearing back

1. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want to be told when something came of it, so that I know the note went somewhere rather than into a void.
2. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want to be told it shipped, so that I can go and use the thing I asked for.
3. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want to be told plainly when it is not planned, so that I stop waiting for something that is not coming.
4. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want to be told when the thing I asked for already exists, so that I can be shown where it is rather than assuming the app cannot do it.
5. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want the message to arrive without my going to look for it, so that being heard does not depend on my checking a page.
6. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want to see all my past Notes and what came of each, so that I can tell at a glance which ones are still open.
7. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want that list to sit where I write new ones, so that I see what came of the last one at the moment I am about to write the next.
8. As someone who has never left a Feedback Note, I want the page to look as it does today, so that an empty list is not a section of nothing.
9. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want the message to read in the app's own voice rather than as a support-desk reply, so that it sounds like the team and not a helpdesk.
10. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want tapping the notification to take me to my Notes, so that I can see which one it was about.

### Setting an Outcome without extra work

11. As a Full-timer, I want closing the issue behind a Note to set its Outcome, so that telling someone costs me nothing beyond the close I was doing anyway.
12. As a Full-timer, I want closing an issue as completed to mean "it shipped", so that the ordinary close is the ordinary good news.
13. As a Full-timer, I want closing an issue as not planned to mean "we are not doing this", so that the decline is recorded by the same action that records it for me.
14. As a Full-timer, I want one label — `already-exists` — to mean "this is already in the app", so that the only Outcome with no free signal costs one click rather than a second pass.
15. As a Full-timer, I want the label to win over the close reason when both are present, so that labelling deliberately is not overridden by how I happened to close.
16. As a Full-timer, I want never to be asked to write a sentence to a submitter, so that this mechanism does not decay into one I stop using.
17. As a Full-timer, I want no reply box on the admin list, so that the absence is obviously deliberate rather than unfinished.
18. As a Full-timer, I want marking a Note resolved in the admin list to reach the submitter the same way, so that there is one path to an Outcome and not two.

### Outcome as its own fact

19. As a developer, I want Outcome stored beside `status` rather than folded into it, so that adding a pipeline state later does not force a decision about what to tell a user.
20. As a Full-timer, I want `status` to keep meaning what it means today, so that the admin list's existing filters are undisturbed.
21. As a Full-timer, I want a Note's Outcome to be set once and cleared only by a reopen, so that it does not flap as I tidy issues.
22. As a developer, I want the Outcome vocabulary to live in the shared core module, so that web and mobile cannot disagree about what an Outcome is.
23. As a developer, I want the three sentences to live beside that vocabulary, so that changing the wording is one edit in one place.
24. As a Full-timer, I want Notes carrying no Outcome to read as "still open" rather than as anything having been decided, so that silence is not mistaken for a decision.

### Not planned is an answer, not an archive

25. As a Full-timer, I want a not-planned Note to stay in the active list, so that the decision I most want to be able to explain is the one I can still see.
26. As a Full-timer, I want archiving to remain a separate filing action I take deliberately, so that filing and deciding are not the same gesture.
27. As a Full-timer, I want to archive a not-planned Note when I am done with it, so that the list still clears.
28. As a Full-timer, I want existing Notes that were auto-archived by a not-planned close to be unaffected by this change, so that a behaviour fix does not rewrite history.

### Reopening

29. As a Full-timer, I want reopening an issue to clear the Note's Outcome, so that the app stops claiming something shipped when it did not.
30. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want no second message telling me the first was wrong, so that I do not learn to distrust the first one.
31. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want my Notes list to stop saying "shipped" after a reopen, so that the page and the truth do not disagree.

### Notes that can never be answered

32. As a Full-timer, I want to see which Notes can never reach their author, so that the silence is a known set rather than a surprise.
33. As a Full-timer, I want those Notes marked in the admin list rather than hidden, so that I can follow up out of band if one matters.
34. As a Full-timer, I want no manual send path built for them, so that the exception does not reintroduce the load this whole change removes.

### Privacy

35. As someone who left a Feedback Note, I want my email address kept off the public issue tracker, so that writing to the team does not publish my contact details.
36. As a Full-timer, I want the admin list to keep showing me who wrote a Note, so that removing the address from the issue does not remove it from where I need it.

## Implementation Decisions

**Outcome is a new field on the Feedback record**, beside `status`, not a widening of it. Values: `shipped`, `not-planned`, `already-there`. Absent means no Outcome yet, which reads as "still open". `status` and `archived` keep their current meanings and their current effect on the admin list's filters.

**The Outcome vocabulary and its copy live in the shared core feedback module**, alongside `FEEDBACK_KINDS` and `kindToType`, so web and mobile read one definition. This mirrors the existing convention in that module exactly: pure data and pure mapping functions, with platform-specific icon and colour choices left to each platform. The three sentences are data in that module, not strings inlined at a call site.

**The webhook is the only writer of an Outcome.** On an `issues` event:

- `closed` with the `already-exists` label present → `already-there`
- `closed` with `state_reason: 'not_planned'` → `not-planned`
- `closed` otherwise → `shipped`
- `reopened` → Outcome cleared; `status` continues to become `in_progress` as it does today

The label is checked before the close reason, so deliberate labelling wins.

**`not_planned` no longer sets `archived: true`.** This reverses current webhook behaviour. Archiving becomes only what an admin does explicitly through the update endpoint. Notes already archived by the old behaviour are left alone — no backfill.

**Setting an Outcome writes one notification** into the existing notifications collection, addressed to the Note's `userId`, carrying the sentence for that Outcome and a link to the feedback page. A cleared Outcome writes nothing. Existing notification conventions are followed rather than extended; no new notification type is introduced if an existing one fits the register.

**The submit page grows a list of the signed-in user's own Notes** beneath the composer, showing each Note's message, when it was left, and what came of it. It renders nothing when the user has no Notes. The page's role requirement is unchanged — it is already the lowest role, so everyone who can submit can already reach it.

**The admin list gains two things**: `not-planned` Notes render with a visible Outcome rather than vanishing into the archive, and Notes with no issue URL are marked as unable to reach their author. No reply affordance is added anywhere, deliberately.

**The issue body stops carrying the submitter's email address.** The body needs only enough to identify the Note; the admin list already joins the submitter's name and address from Firestore. Coordinate before implementing — a separate session is scrubbing the addresses already published on existing issues, and this is the forward half of that fix.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts what an actor observes, never how it was arranged: that closing an issue a certain way leaves a Note carrying a particular Outcome and the submitter holding a notification, not that a particular helper was called or a particular shape was passed between functions. Copy is asserted through the shared vocabulary module rather than by matching sentences in a component.

**The Express app, through the existing supertest seam in the server test file.** This is the highest seam available and it already has a full webhook suite driving real HTTP requests against the app with a fake Firestore that can be seeded and read back. Everything on the server side is testable here and nothing new is needed: each close variant producing its Outcome, the label beating the close reason, a reopen clearing it, the notification landing against the right user, and no notification on a clear.

Two existing tests in that suite assert behaviour this spec reverses — the one asserting a `not_planned` close archives the Note, and anything asserting the old status/archive coupling. These are rewritten, not added to. The tests covering the issue body are updated for the removed email address.

**The shared core feedback module, through its existing pure test file.** Outcome vocabulary and copy lookup are pure mappings and test exactly like `kindToType` and `kindMeta` already do there: no mocks, no setup, direct assertions.

**The submit page, through its existing component test file.** That the list renders a user's own Notes with what came of each, that it renders nothing when there are none, and that the composer is unaffected.

**The admin list, through its existing component test file.** That a not-planned Note stays visible with its Outcome shown, that archiving is still reachable as a separate action, and that a Note with no issue URL is marked as unanswerable.

No new test seam is introduced. All four files exist and all four already cover the surfaces being changed.

## Out of Scope

**[#961](https://github.com/Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker/issues/961) itself** — whether the app should gain a way to record a headcount for a Gathering, and whether the figures on the Gatherings page should stop hiding behind an empty missed-list. That is a separate piece of work in its own session. This spec only builds the mechanism that would let someone be told the answer.

**Saying *which* feature already exists.** The `already-there` sentence is generic. Pointing someone at the actual page happens in person, by text, or in Messages. Wiring a feature reference into the Outcome is deliberately not built.

**Any conversation on a Note.** No threads, no comments, no asking a submitter a question in the app. Messages already exists and already accepts a chat attachment of the feedback type; if a lightweight "ask about this" affordance is ever wanted, that is the seam, and it is not this spec.

**Reaching Notes with no issue URL.** They are marked, not answered. No manual send path.

**Scrubbing email addresses from issues already published.** Owned by a separate session. Only the forward fix belongs here.

**Retraction messages on reopen**, and any second notification for a Note whose Outcome changes.

**Drawing response text from issue comments or release notes.** Both were considered and rejected in ADR 0017 — the first as an unreviewed pipe from a public tracker to a named user, the second because nothing links an issue to a release.

## Further Notes

The glossary carries the vocabulary this spec uses: **Feedback Note**, **Outcome (of a Feedback Note)** and **What came of it**, the last two added alongside ADR 0017. The Feedback Note entry has always listed `_Avoid_: bug ticket, customer support issue, help desk ticket`, and the new entries extend that stance — `_Avoid_: reply, response, resolution message, support reply`. Copy written for this feature should sound like the rest of the app ("Tell us how it's going", "gone quiet", "We missed"), not like a ticketing system.

Three things were wanted at once here and could not all be had: a response the user finds meaningful, no authoring load on the maintainer, and assurance the user trusts. A fully automatic message can only ever say that the work behind a Note closed. The bet this spec makes is that a thin message which always arrives beats a good one that arrives sometimes. If that bet proves wrong, the place to revisit it is the copy and the `already-there` Outcome, not the mechanism.

The webhook matches Notes by issue URL and updates every match, so Notes sharing an issue all receive the same Outcome. That is intended.

title: Spec: Reporter labels and email redaction for feedback-created GitHub issues
label: OPEN
body:
## Problem Statement

People submit **Feedback Notes** from CISA Campus Work Tracker. The server mirrors each note to a GitHub issue, but the issue currently exposes the reporter's full name and email in the body and has no reporter label. This makes issues hard to filter by reporter and publishes personal contact information in a public repository. Admins can also manually create an issue with the same exposed fields, and existing feedback-created issues already contain these emails.

## Solution

Give every feedback-created GitHub issue a public reporter label of `reporter:<first-name>-<last-initial>` and reduce the issue body attribution to first name only. Stop publishing email and surnames. Backfill existing feedback-created issues so current public bodies and snapshots no longer expose email. Stop storing email on new Feedback Notes, while retaining historical emails privately in Firestore and keeping full names available to admins. Anonymous feedback receives no label and `Anonymous` in the body. The admin manual "Create Issue" fallback follows the same public rules.

## User Stories

1. As a campus minister, I want my Feedback Note to become a GitHub issue attributed only by my first name, so that my surname and email are not published.
2. As a campus minister, I want the issue to carry a reporter label, so that the team can filter GitHub issues by who submitted them.
3. As a campus minister who shares a first name with another reporter, I want the label to include a last-name initial, so that our issues remain distinguishable.
4. As a campus minister whose display name has no last name, I want the label to fall back to first name only, so that my feedback still has attribution.
5. As a campus minister whose Firebase profile has no usable display name, I want the issue to say `Anonymous` and carry no reporter label, so that no false identity is invented.
6. As a campus minister, I want no email address to appear anywhere in the public issue body, so that the public repository does not expose my contact details.
7. As a campus minister, I want new Feedback Notes to stop storing my email, so that future collection honors the stated privacy boundary.
8. As an admin, I want reporters' full names to remain available privately in the app, so that I can still understand who submitted a note when following up.
9. As an admin, I want legacy Firestore feedback documents to keep their historical email addresses, so that existing admin lookup behavior does not break.
10. As an admin, I want new feedback documents to omit email, so that the data model matches the privacy decision.
11. As an admin, I want existing feedback-created GitHub issues to receive reporter labels and scrubbed bodies, so that historical issues are as filterable and private as new ones.
12. As an admin, I want the backfill to run as an idempotent, dry-run-first operation, so that public issue edits can be reviewed before they happen.
13. As an admin, I want backfill to skip issues with no parseable reporter data and report them, so that the script never guesses attribution.
14. As an admin, I want the manual "Create Issue" fallback to omit email and surname and to include the reporter label when available, so that the fallback is not a privacy bypass.
15. As an admin, I want the Feedback list to keep showing email for legacy documents when present, so that existing records remain useful.
16. As an admin, I want the Feedback list to work when a new document has no email, so that missing email does not break rendering or search.
17. As an operator, I want reporter labels to be created automatically before issue creation, so that authors do not have to maintain labels manually.
18. As an operator, I want a label-creation failure to still allow the issue to be created, so that GitHub label problems never block a person from submitting feedback.
19. As an operator, I want reporter labels to have deterministic colours and no descriptions, so that labels are visually distinct without adding public metadata.
20. As an operator, I want each reporter to have a stable stored label, so that future submissions reuse the same label rather than recomputing attribution.
21. As an operator, I want same-first-and-last-initial collisions to receive `-2`, `-3`, and so on, so that two different reporters are not merged into one label.
22. As an operator, I want historical reporter labels mapped best-effort from existing issue data, so that backfill is safe even where user identity cannot be linked to a Firebase UID.
23. As a developer, I want one shared reporter-attribution helper used by the API, migration script, admin fallback, and backfill, so that all paths produce the same public result.
24. As a developer, I want feedback schema, rules, and types to treat email as optional and to allow an optional private reporter label, so that new no-email documents are valid.
25. As a developer, I want tests at the existing API, migration, UI, and Firestore-rules seams rather than new seams, so that the feature is verified without adding architectural surface area.
26. As a privacy owner, I want an ADR recording public first-name/last-initial attribution, private legacy email retention, and the decision not to rewrite Git history, so that future readers understand the trade-off.
27. As a sync consumer, I want the tracked GitHub issue snapshots regenerated after backfill, so that the current repository files no longer contain those emails.
28. As a project maintainer, I want the known residual limits documented, so that no one claims the purge removed GitHub internal edit history, notifications, forks, or old Git blobs.

## Implementation Decisions

### Public attribution contract

- A reporter label is always `reporter:<first-name>-<last-initial>`, normalised to lowercase and strips characters that are not safe in a GitHub label name.
- If the display name has no last name, the label falls back to `reporter:<first-name>`.
- The public issue body uses `- **Submitted By:** <first-name>` only. It does not include a surname or email address.
- No `@mention`, no GitHub assignee, and no attempt to change the issue author is part of this feature.
- Missing or unusable display names produce `- **Submitted By:** Anonymous` and no reporter label.
- Anonymous reporters do not receive a shared `reporter:anonymous` label.

### Reporter label lifecycle

- A private `reporterLabel` field is persisted on the reporter's user profile so the same label is reused on future submissions.
- If the base label is already claimed by a different user profile, a numeric suffix is added: `reporter:tony-w`, `reporter:tony-w-2`, and so on.
- A deterministic colour is derived from the label name. Reporter labels have no description.
- The reporter label is created in the GitHub repository before the issue is created.
- Label creation is fail-open: if label creation or assignment fails, the issue is still created and the failure is logged.
- New feedback documents may also record the private `reporterLabel` so the admin manual fallback can reuse the exact label.

### API and issue creation

- The feedback API continues to authenticate the Firebase user.
- It stops persisting `userEmail` on new feedback documents.
- It continues to persist the reporter's full `userName` privately for admin use.
- It derives the public first-name attribution and reporter label from the authenticated user's profile.
- It adds the reporter label to the issue's label set alongside the existing type label and `feedback`.
- If the reporter label is unavailable or the reporter is anonymous, the issue is created without that label.

### Migration and manual fallback

- The bulk migration path uses the same reporter-attribution helper, omits email, applies the reporter label, and records the private reporter label on the migrated feedback document.
- The admin manual "Create Issue" fallback uses first-name-only attribution, omits email, and includes the stored reporter label when present.
- If the manual fallback derives a label that does not yet exist, it must not block opening the prefilled issue page.

### Historical backfill

- A one-off backfill targets GitHub issues with the `feedback` label or a `[Feedback]` title.
- It parses the existing `Submitted By` line to recover the reporter's full name.
- It ensures each reporter label exists, patches the issue body to remove surname and email, and adds the reporter label without disturbing existing labels.
- Historical labels are assigned best-effort by full name. Different full names with the same base label receive collision suffixes; unresolvable historical labels may merge later.
- Issues with no parseable reporter data are skipped and reported.
- The backfill defaults to dry-run and requires an explicit execute flag before any GitHub write. It is idempotent and safe to rerun.
- The current tracked issue snapshots are regenerated after a successful backfill. Snapshot refresh must be reviewable and must not auto-push to the main branch.

### Data model

- New feedback documents may omit `userEmail`.
- Existing feedback documents keep their historical `userEmail` values untouched.
- An optional private `reporterLabel` field is allowed on feedback documents and user profiles.
- Full reporter names remain private in Firestore and in the admin UI.
- The change is recorded as an ADR. No domain-glossary term is added because reporter labels are a GitHub implementation artifact rather than a project domain concept.

### Explicitly rejected alternatives

- Making the reporter the GitHub issue author is rejected because it requires a different GitHub authentication architecture.
- Assigning the issue to the reporter is rejected because reporters are not necessarily GitHub collaborators.
- `@mention` attribution is rejected because no GitHub username is collected and most reporters do not have one.
- Git history rewriting is rejected. Historical blobs may remain in repository history.
- Purging existing Firestore emails is rejected. They remain private so admin lookup and historical context keep working.

## Testing Decisions

Good tests assert externally visible behaviour: the HTTP response, the request sent to the GitHub API, the rendered admin UI, the resulting Firestore document shape, or the result of the public helper functions. Tests should not assert private implementation details such as helper call order when an observable result is enough.

The testing seams are:

- The feedback HTTP endpoint, using the existing server API tests with mocked GitHub fetch and in-memory Firestore.
- The pure reporter-attribution helpers, using unit tests for normalisation, first-name fallback, anonymous handling, and collision suffixes.
- The bulk migration function, using the existing migration-script tests with mocked GitHub fetch and a fake Firestore.
- The one-off backfill script, using a new external seam at the GitHub API boundary with mocked fetch. This is a new seam because the script is a new executable operation; it should not introduce a parallel in-app abstraction.
- The admin Feedback list and feedback submission components, using the existing component tests.
- Firestore rules, using the existing rules test seam to prove new feedback documents without email are valid while legacy documents with email remain readable.

Prior art in the codebase:

- Server endpoint tests already mock GitHub issue creation and inspect the outgoing request body and labels.
- Migration-script tests already exercise the issue-creation path through a fake Firestore.
- Feedback UI tests already render the Feedback list and check the manual issue URL.
- Firestore rules tests already validate feedback document shapes.

## Out of Scope

- Changing GitHub issue authorship, assignment, or mentions.
- Rewriting Git history to remove old snapshots.
- Purging historical email addresses from Firestore.
- Guaranteeing removal from GitHub internal edit history, prior notifications, forks, or third-party archives.
- Labelling the two feedback-labelled issues that have no parseable reporter data.
- Reworking the Feedback Note kinds, labels, statuses, or screenshot flow.
- Changing contact Tags or any other domain concept that uses the word "tag".

## Further Notes

- The GitHub token used for issue creation and backfill needs write access to issues and labels.
- Rollout order: implement code and tests; run the standard verification commands; run the backfill dry-run and review the proposed 126 updates and 2 skips; execute the backfill only after explicit approval; regenerate snapshots without auto-push; deploy the server and UI changes.
- The ADR should record the privacy trade-off, the first-name/last-initial public attribution, the private legacy-email decision, and the residual limitations.
- Known residual limits after this work: old tracked snapshots remain in Git history; GitHub's internal edit history and already-sent notifications are not fully controllable; historical labels mapped only by name may merge if two different people share the same first name and last initial; the two unparseable historical issues remain without a reporter label.

title: Attendance moves onto the Gathering (destination, not scheduled)
label: OPEN

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Awaiting initial triage by a maintainer

body:
> **Not scheduled.** Filed to record a decision made while specifying the Gatherings redesign, so the destination is written down rather than rediscovered. Needs its own design pass before anyone picks it up.

## Problem Statement

Attendance is stored on the wrong side of the relationship.

A Contact carries a map of Gathering id to attendance state. To answer "who was at Wednesday Bible Study," the page loads every Contact in the organisation and scans their maps — once per chip, across a whole term. The Gathering itself holds no record of what happened at it.

This inversion is the reason for several things that look like independent problems:

- **A Gathering cannot say it was empty.** "We held it and nobody came" and "nobody has opened this one" are both an absence of matching entries. Attendance-taken stamps were added to the Gathering specifically to paper over this — they exist because the Gathering had no attendance record of its own that could legitimately be empty.
- **Counting is a full-collection scan.** Present counts for a term of chips mean walking every Contact for every week.
- **A Gathering is not self-describing.** Reading one tells you nothing about who was there; the answer is distributed across hundreds of other documents.

## Solution

Move attendance onto the Gathering, so that the record of an occasion lives on the occasion.

A Gathering holds who was present, who was absent, and who arrived late. An empty present list becomes a legitimate, meaningful value — the room was empty — distinguishable from a Gathering nobody has marked by whether the record exists at all, which retires the attendance-taken stamps.

## User Stories

1. As a Full-timer, I want a Gathering to record who was there, so that the occasion is self-describing.
2. As a Full-timer, I want "we met and nobody came" to be a value rather than an inference, so that an empty room is a fact.
3. As a Full-timer, I want a week's present count to be a field on that week, so that a term of chips does not require scanning every contact in the organisation.
4. As a Full-timer, I want the attendance-taken stamps retired once they are redundant, so that there are not two sources of truth about whether a week was marked.
5. As a Full-timer, I want "Who we've missed lately" to keep working exactly as it does, so that a storage change is invisible to me.
6. As a Full-timer, I want a newcomer's absences before they joined to keep not counting against them, so that ADR 0005's no-retroactive-penalty rule survives the move.
7. As a Full-timer, I want follow-up suggestions driven by absence to keep working, so that the missed-list's downstream behaviour is unchanged.
8. As a maintainer, I want the migration to be reversible until it is verified, so that a bad cutover is recoverable.
9. As a maintainer, I want both read paths to work during the migration, so that the app is never mid-broken.

## Implementation Decisions

Deliberately thin — this needs a design pass before it is specified properly. What is settled:

**The direction is Gathering-owned**, not a denormalised mirror in both places as a permanent state. A mirror may be the migration mechanism; it is not the destination.

**This retires the attendance-taken stamps** rather than keeping them alongside. Two records of whether a week was marked is worse than either.

**The reverse read still needs an answer.** "Which Gatherings has this Contact missed" is the query behind the missed list, the absence streaks and the follow-up suggestions, and it reads in the direction that Contact-keyed storage was good at. Deciding how that is served — a query, a maintained per-Contact summary, or something else — is the substance of the design pass, and is why this is not simply a schema swap.

**The migration is dual-write then cut over**, verified before the old path is removed.

**ADR 0005 is in scope.** Its no-retroactive-penalty rule and its "We missed" scoping are defined against the current storage and must be restated, not merely preserved by accident.

## Testing Decisions

To be determined by the design pass. The constraint known now: the missed-list behaviour, the absence streaks and the no-retroactive-penalty rule all need characterisation tests written **before** the move, against current behaviour, so the migration has something to be correct against.

## Out of Scope

Everything in the Gatherings page redesign, which is specced separately and deliberately does not depend on this. That redesign keeps Contact-keyed attendance and continues to use the attendance-taken stamps.

## Further Notes

Vocabulary is in `CONTEXT.md`: **Gathering**, **Attendance taken**.

This was identified while grilling the Gatherings redesign and consciously deferred: folding it in would have roughly tripled that issue's scope and put a data migration in the middle of a UI change. Filed so it is not lost.

title: Gatherings: Rhythm becomes a record, the kind is retired, and the page reorders around this week
label: OPEN
body:
## Problem Statement

The Gatherings page is organised around a concept it cannot represent.

A **Rhythm** — the Wednesday Bible Study, the Thursday College Meeting — is the thing a Full-timer actually thinks in. It has a name, a cadence, a place it meets, and a roster of who usually comes. None of that is stored. A Rhythm is inferred at read time from a chain of sibling Gathering documents, each carrying its own copy of the name, kind, location and roster. So:

- **The roster is set per week, not per Rhythm.** Adding a regular means editing every remaining week, which is why a confirm prompt asks "this one, or all future?" on every roster change — a decision interrupting an action that should be ordinary.
- **A cadence exists only as loose fields on each occurrence.** There is nowhere to say "this runs every Wednesday until December", so a term cannot be extended; it can only be re-created.
- **A week that did not happen cannot be recorded.** Cancelling means deleting the Gathering, which leaves no trace. "We didn't meet" and "this week was never scheduled" are the same absence.
- **Deleting the first Gathering orphans the rest**, because identity hangs off a real record rather than its own.

Alongside this sits a taxonomy that no longer earns its place. Every Gathering carries a **kind** (`Weekly`, `Small Group`, `Special`, `Outreach`) from a managed collection with its own Settings section and editing modal. It buys a row of filter pills that narrow three Rhythms to three Rhythms, a subtitle reading "Weekly" under "Wednesday Bible Study", and a one-line blurb per kind that is rendered by nothing — it is called only by its own tests. The seeded defaults describe a Friday fellowship the team does not run. Kinds are referenced by name, so renaming one rewrites every Gathering carrying the old string.

The shared calendar is also wired into this page in a way that contradicts how the team uses it. Categories map onto gathering kinds through a setting held in `localStorage` — per browser, so two Full-timers can disagree about what counts as a gathering — and calendar events in those categories render on the page as Gatherings, which are things this app takes attendance for. They are not.

Finally the page reads in the wrong order. "Who we've missed lately" — reflection — sits above "This week", which is what a Full-timer opens the page on a gathering evening to act on. The section holding the Rhythms is called "When we met", past tense, while carrying chips that run to December. "Coming up" duplicates what those future chips already say.

## Solution

**Make a Rhythm a record.** `Rhythm` owns the name, the cadence, the location and the roster. Each Gathering carries a reference to its Rhythm plus the facts particular to that occasion — its date, who was there, whether attendance was taken, and whether it happened at all. The cadence is generative: a term can be extended, and missing occurrences repaired, without re-creating anything.

**Retire the kind.** A Rhythm's name and cadence say what it is. The `type` field, the managed collection, its Settings section, its editing modal and the filter pills all go.

**Draw the line at the shared calendar by audience.** This app tracks what needs attendance taken; the calendar tracks what other people need to see. Those sets are disjoint, so the calendar's gathering branch is deleted — it contributes context items and away/OOO only, which is what the "Also on the calendar" section already exists for.

**Reorder the page around the weekly act.** This week → What we run → One-offs → Who we've missed lately → Also on the calendar.

A design canvas covering the redesigned page, the Rhythm row anatomy and the shipped page's current behaviour is in `docs/design/gathering-page/`.

## User Stories

### The Rhythm as a record

1. As a Full-timer, I want a Rhythm to be a thing I can open and edit, so that "who usually comes" is set once rather than per week.
2. As a Full-timer, I want the expected roster to belong to the Rhythm, so that adding a regular reaches every week from now on in one action.
3. As a Full-timer, I want to change one week's roster without changing the Rhythm's, so that a one-off guest does not become a regular.
4. As a Full-timer, I want the "this one or all future?" prompt gone from ordinary roster edits, so that marking attendance is not interrupted by a decision.
5. As a Full-timer, I want a roster change to reach weeks that are still ahead even if I once edited one of them, so that a new regular is not silently dropped from a week I happened to touch.
6. As a Full-timer, I want weeks that have already happened to keep the roster they had, so that history does not move when I change who comes now.
7. As a Full-timer, I want a Rhythm to carry where it usually meets, so that I set the room once.
8. As a Full-timer, I want a week I moved to keep the room it actually met in, so that "we met in the chapel that week" stays true after the Rhythm's usual room changes.
9. As a Full-timer, I want renaming a Rhythm to rename it everywhere including past weeks, so that the row's title and its chips never disagree about what this thing is called.
10. As a Full-timer, I want a Rhythm to store its cadence, so that the schedule is a fact about the Rhythm rather than a shape I have to infer from its occurrences.
11. As a Full-timer, I want to extend a Rhythm's term, so that continuing into spring is one action rather than re-creating the whole thing.
12. As a Full-timer, I want missing occurrences in a term to be repairable, so that a half-created term can be completed without starting over.
13. As a Full-timer, I want deleting one Gathering to leave the Rhythm intact, so that removing a week does not orphan every week after it.

### Weeks that did not happen

14. As a Full-timer, I want to mark that we did not meet on a given week, so that a cancelled week is a fact rather than a deletion.
15. As a Full-timer, I want a cancelled week to count nobody absent, so that a snow day does not appear in anyone's missed streak.
16. As a Full-timer, I want a cancelled week to read differently from a week nobody has marked, so that "we didn't meet" and "nobody has got to this one" are never the same answer.
17. As a Full-timer, I want to undo a cancellation, so that "we did meet after all" does not require re-creating the week.
18. As a Full-timer, I want to see the weeks a Rhythm did not meet in one place, so that I can review them without walking the strip.

### The page

19. As a Full-timer opening the page on a gathering evening, I want this week's Gatherings first on the page, so that the thing I came to do is not below a section about the past.
20. As a Full-timer, I want the section holding my Rhythms to have a name that is not past tense, so that a list containing December does not call itself "when we met".
21. As a Full-timer, I want each Rhythm to occupy one row carrying its whole term as chips, so that I can see the arc at a glance.
22. As a Full-timer, I want a chip to show whether attendance was taken, so that gaps in the term are visible without opening anything.
23. As a Full-timer, I want this week's chip marked distinctly, so that I find the current week by looking rather than by counting dates.
24. As a Full-timer, I want weeks still ahead shown faintly, so that I can tell what has happened from what has not.
25. As a Full-timer, I want a cancelled chip struck through rather than given its own colour, so that it reads as the week not being there rather than as a fifth kind of attendance.
26. As a Full-timer, I want the strip to stay usable when a term is long, so that extending a Rhythm through spring does not break the row.
27. As a Full-timer, I want one control that returns the strip to the current week, so that I can get back after looking at October.
28. As a Full-timer, I want that control to be quiet when I am already on this week, so that it is not shouting at me by default.
29. As a Full-timer, I want to select any chip and see that week's summary without leaving the row, so that checking an earlier week is not a navigation.
30. As a Full-timer, I want a marked chip to show how many of the expected roster came, so that a thin week is visible without opening it.
31. As a Full-timer, I want the Rhythm row's subtitle to say its cadence and where it meets, so that two Rhythms sharing a weekday are told apart at a glance.
32. As a Full-timer, I want Rhythm rows ordered by day of week and kept in that order, so that I learn where Wednesday lives and stop reading the page.
33. As a Full-timer, I want two Rhythms falling on the same date grouped under one date heading in the week band, so that I mark both in one sitting.
34. As a Full-timer, I want a week with no Gatherings to say so plainly, so that an empty band reads as "nothing on" rather than a page that failed.
35. As a Full-timer, I want one-off Gatherings listed separately below the Rhythms, so that a Welcome BBQ is not filed among things that repeat.
36. As a Full-timer, I want a one-off still ahead shown faintly in that same list, so that a retreat in October is visible somewhere rather than nowhere.
37. As a Full-timer, I want "Who we've missed lately" below the Rhythms, so that reflection follows the doing.
38. As a Full-timer, I want the figures beside that list sized by their own content and each separated from the next, so that the section reads as one composed row and I can read one number without reading all three.

### Creating

39. As a Full-timer, I want starting a Rhythm and logging a one-off to be two clearly separate acts, so that I am not choosing between them with a toggle halfway down a form.
40. As a Full-timer, I want the one-off form to be short, so that logging a barbecue does not present me with cadence and roster fields it will never use.
41. As a Full-timer, I want the Rhythm form to ask for the roster once, so that setting up "who usually comes" happens at creation rather than on the first week.

### Roster editing

42. As a Full-timer, I want to search the whole contact directory when adding someone to a Rhythm's roster, so that I am not limited to people already involved.
43. As a Full-timer, I want to create a contact from the roster editor by typing a name, so that a newcomer can be added without leaving what I am doing.
44. As a Full-timer, I want removing someone from a roster to be recoverable, so that a mis-tap does not quietly change who counts as missed.
45. As a Full-timer, I want the expected count to update everywhere at once when I change a roster, so that the drawer, the row and the week band never disagree.

### The kind, and the calendar

46. As a Full-timer, I want the kind filters and their Settings section gone, so that I am not maintaining a taxonomy that narrows three rows to three rows.
47. As a Full-timer, I want Gatherings created before this change to keep working without their kind, so that history stays readable.
48. As a Full-timer, I want calendar events to stop appearing as Gatherings, so that the page holds only things we take attendance for.
49. As a Full-timer, I want calendar events to keep appearing as context, so that I still know the club fair is on Saturday.
50. As a Full-timer, I want the decision about which calendar categories matter to stop living in my browser, so that my colleague and I see the same page.

### Roles

51. As a Full-timer, I want the roster to stay gated to Full-timers, so that the recent fix keeping the contact directory away from Community is not undone.

## Implementation Decisions

**Rhythm becomes a stored record**, owning `name`, `cadence`, `location` and `roster`. Each Gathering references its Rhythm. The derived-anchor scheme (`parentEventId` falling back to own id) is replaced, not extended — but only after the stopgap that makes it work lands, so the page is never worse than it is today during this work.

**The Gathering keeps what is particular to the occasion**: its date, attendance stamps, a roster override where one exists, its own location where the week moved, and a cancelled state.

**Name reads through; location snapshots.** A name is identity, so renaming applies everywhere including past weeks. A location is a fact about an occasion, so a week that met elsewhere keeps where it met. These deliberately get different answers.

**Roster resolution is: the Rhythm's roster, with a per-Gathering override applied on top, frozen for Gatherings in the past.** A past Gathering carries its roster as it stood. A future Gathering resolves live from the Rhythm each time, with any override re-applied — so editing one future week does not amputate it from later Rhythm changes. This is the rule that retires the confirm prompt and the clean form of what ADR 0005 intended.

**Cadence is generative.** The Rhythm can extend its term, writing further Gatherings, and a repair pass can fill occurrences the cadence implies but that do not exist. Occurrences are still materialised as documents up front — lazy materialisation was considered and rejected, because chips, rosters and the public RSVP card all need occurrences that exist.

**Cancelling is a state on the Gathering, never a deletion.** A cancelled Gathering counts nobody absent and is excluded from attendance figures. It is entered from the selected week's summary — where the Full-timer already is when practice is called off — and reviewed or undone from the Rhythm's drawer.

**Chip state is a five-way enum** computed in the view model: attendance taken; happened but not taken; falls in the current week; still ahead; cancelled. Deriving "taken" from an empty present list stays rejected — it permanently mislabels a week nobody attended.

**The kind is deleted outright**: the `type` field, the managed collection, its Settings section, its editing modal, and the filter pills. Existing Gatherings keep whatever string they carry until it is dropped; nothing reads it. This reverses #776's story 28, which was written to protect a feature now judged not worth protecting.

**The calendar's gathering branch is deleted**: the category-to-kind mapping, its `localStorage` store, the gathering item type and the merge that blended calendar events into the page's Gathering lists. The calendar keeps contributing context items and away/OOO, gated as today. The line is by audience — this app tracks what needs attendance, the calendar tracks what others need to see — and those sets do not overlap.

**Page order becomes** This week → What we run → One-offs → Who we've missed lately → Also on the calendar. "Coming up" is removed; future chips and faint one-off rows carry what it said.

**The Rhythm row's subtitle is cadence plus location.** Nothing replaces the filter pills; the section heading simply sits closer to the rows.

**The chip strip windows around the current week** and scrolls horizontally, with the return-to-today control doubling as the anchor. That control is quiet when the selection is already on this week and prominent once it is not.

**Configuring a Rhythm moves to a drawer** — name, cadence, location, roster, extend the term, and the list of cancelled weeks. Taking attendance stays inline on the row. The split is by frequency: marking happens weekly, configuring happens twice a term. A drawer rather than a page so the Rhythm list stays visible behind it.

**Creating splits into two acts** — "Start a Rhythm" and "Log a gathering" — chosen before any fields appear, not via a toggle inside one form. The one-off form loses cadence and roster entirely.

**The roster editor searches the whole contact directory** and can create a contact from a typed name, per ADR 0005's walk-in rule. Removal needs an undo; the exact affordance is the implementer's call.

**Types are unified.** There are currently two `Event` definitions that have drifted — the web one carries `roster` and the attendance stamps, the shared one does not, so mobile structurally cannot see either. The shared package becomes the single definition and the web type re-exports it. `Event` is renamed to `Gathering` in types and variables; the Firestore collection keeps its name, because migrating a collection name buys nothing.

**The model lands on all three surfaces** — web, `AttendanceMobile`, and the native Gatherings screen — since all three read these records. The UX redesign in this issue is web only.

## Testing Decisions

A good test asserts what a Full-timer would notice: that this week's Gatherings are named at the top, that a Rhythm appears once, that a cancelled week counts nobody absent, that a roster change reaches a future week and not a past one. It does not assert class names, element order within a row, or that a helper was called.

**Two existing seams carry the logic, and no new seam is introduced.**

`buildGatheringViewModel` takes everything page-shaped: it grows one input (the Rhythms) alongside the Gatherings, the Contacts and the instant, and returns the whole view model — the week band grouped by date, the Rhythms in day-of-week order with their chips and selection, the one-offs including future ones. Cancelled as a fifth chip state, the cadence-and-location subtitle and the strip's windowing anchor are all computed here. The view renders that model and holds no grouping, week-bounding or chip-state logic of its own. Prior art and home for these tests: `gatheringViewModel.test.ts`.

`attendanceRoster` takes series identity and roster resolution: which Gatherings belong to a Rhythm, and the Rhythm-roster-plus-override-with-past-freeze rule. It lives here rather than in the view model because marking attendance needs it too, and the mark path should not depend on a render-shaped module. Prior art: `attendanceRoster.test.ts`.

**Cases worth writing**, all pure: a week containing two Gatherings on one date; a week containing none; a cancelled Gathering excluded from attendance figures and from missed streaks; a Gathering with attendance taken and nobody present versus one never opened; a Gathering dated on a week boundary; ordering across three Rhythms on two weekdays; one-offs excluded from Rhythm grouping and future one-offs included in their list; a roster edit on a future Gathering that still picks up a later Rhythm change; a roster edit on a past Gathering that does not; a renamed Rhythm changing a past week's title while that week keeps its own location.

**View tests assert wiring only** — the band names this week's Gatherings, a Rhythm renders one row, selecting a chip changes the summary shown, the drawer opens with the Rhythm's roster, removing someone updates the expected count in the row behind it. Prior art: `Attendance.test.tsx` and `AttendanceRhythms.test.tsx`.

**The alignment and ordering changes get no tests.** They are styling and section order with no assertable behaviour, and per the project's testing policy a snapshot written to satisfy the policy is worse than no test.

**Firestore rules changes need CI.** Rules tests skip locally without JDK 21, so a rules change is only proven by a CI run.

## Out of Scope

- **The `parentEventId` stopgap**, specced as its own issue and shipping ahead of this one.
- **Moving attendance onto the Gathering.** Attendance currently lives on the Contact, keyed by Gathering id, which is why counting a week means scanning every Contact and why the attendance-taken stamps exist at all. Moving it is the right destination and is filed separately; folding it in here would triple the scope and touch the missed-list, the absence metrics and ADR 0005's no-retroactive-penalty rule.
- **Mobile UX.** The model change lands on all surfaces; the mobile page redesign does not. A term-long chip strip does not survive 390px by shrinking — it needs its own design.
- **Publishing to the shared calendar.** The app-owns-Gatherings direction makes a one-way publish cheap later. Not now, and nothing here should assume it.
- **Rule-based recurrence** — storing only a cadence and materialising a Gathering when attendance is taken. Considered and rejected: chips, rosters and the RSVP card all need occurrences that exist.
- **A calendar view** of the page. With three Rhythms on two weekdays it is mostly empty cells.
- **A debt queue** ordering the page by what still needs marking. Designed and dropped in favour of ordering by Rhythm.
- **The light-theme radius token collision** — `.light` re-declares two radius tokens, overriding the ladder ADR 0009 established, so `rounded-xl` and `rounded-2xl` both render 32px in light and differently in dark. Real, unrelated, worth its own issue.

## Further Notes

Vocabulary is in `CONTEXT.md`: **Gathering** (one occasion attendance is taken for), **Rhythm** (a Gathering that repeats, and now a record in its own right), **Attendance taken**, **Cancelled**.

Note the collision that is not one: a Bible Study is both a **Study** (the materials arc, its weeks being **Meetings**) and a **Rhythm** (the schedule its Gatherings hang off). Separate objects on separate pages — College Meeting is a Rhythm with no Study, and a Meeting is explicitly not an attendance record. Do not merge them.

**ADR 0005** governs roster semantics and still holds. It should be amended when the roster actually moves onto the Rhythm — not before — to replace "recurring instances inherit the series roster, and admins are prompted per edit" with the resolution rule above.

**ADR 0011** rejected binding a Bible Study Entry point to a Rhythm on the grounds that a Rhythm is derived rather than stored and has no identity of its own. This issue makes that premise false. The decision still stands for independent reasons — an Entry point needs a durable slug outliving every Study, and binding to a Rhythm would make the QR depend on that Rhythm surviving — so 0011 is annotated rather than reopened.

**#776 story 27** asked for Trainees to open this page without admin rights. It was never implementable: route access closes `/attendance` to Trainees and the Trainee drawer deliberately omits Gatherings. The story is struck rather than built.

Design canvas: `docs/design/gathering-page/`.

title: Gatherings: recurring terms never group into a Rhythm — parentEventId has no writer
label: CLOSED
body:
## Problem Statement

A Full-timer opens `/attendance` expecting the Rhythm rows that #776 shipped — one row per thing the team runs, carrying its whole term as a strip of chips. They do not exist. Instead the page shows one flat row per occurrence, all wearing the same three names, and every Gathering dated after today is missing from the page entirely.

The team runs three Rhythms: Bible Study on Wednesday, Bible Study on Thursday, and College Meeting on Thursday. A term of those is 48 Gatherings. The page renders the handful that have already happened as unrelated one-offs and silently drops the rest.

Two other features fail from the same cause:

- **"Apply roster update to all future gatherings in this series?"** updates only the Gathering the Full-timer opened. The prompt has been describing work it does not do.
- The Rhythm-shaped tests all pass, so nothing has flagged any of this.

## Solution

Write the field that identifies a Rhythm when a recurring term is created, and backfill it for terms created before this change.

`parentEventId` has no writer anywhere in the repository. Every reference to it is a read, a type declaration, or a test fixture. Creating a recurring term writes N sibling Gathering documents — each carrying `isRecurring: true`, a copied name, kind, location and roster — and never links them to each other. Series identity then falls back to each document's own id, so every group holds exactly one Gathering and the is-a-series test fails on both of its branches. Each occurrence drops through to the one-off list; future ones are removed by the past-tense filter and appear nowhere.

The fix is small and shippable on its own, ahead of any redesign: set the anchor when the batch is written, and run a one-time backfill that groups existing siblings into series.

## User Stories

1. As a Full-timer, I want a recurring Bible Study to occupy one row rather than one row per week, so that the list of what we do is as short as the number of things we actually do.
2. As a Full-timer, I want every Gathering in the term to appear as a chip on its Rhythm's strip, so that I can see the whole arc without opening anything.
3. As a Full-timer, I want Gatherings scheduled after today to be visible somewhere on the page, so that a term running to December does not look like it ends this week.
4. As a Full-timer, I want the terms I created before this fix to group correctly too, so that I do not have to delete and re-create a term to get a working page.
5. As a Full-timer, I want "apply to all future gatherings in this series" to actually reach all future gatherings, so that a roster change I make once does not silently apply to one week.
6. As a Full-timer, I want the two Thursday Rhythms to stay separate rows, so that Bible Study and College Meeting are not merged just because they share a weekday.
7. As a Full-timer, I want a one-off Gathering to stay a one-off after the backfill, so that a Welcome BBQ is not absorbed into a series it never belonged to.
8. As a Full-timer, I want the backfill to be safe to run more than once, so that a partial run can be repeated without creating new problems.
9. As a maintainer, I want a test that fails against the current creation path, so that this class of defect — a read with no writer — cannot pass review again.
10. As a maintainer, I want the grouping rule to be a pure function rather than logic inside a modal, so that it can be tested without rendering a form.

## Implementation Decisions

**The anchor is the first Gathering of the batch.** When a recurring term is written, every document in the batch carries `parentEventId` set to the id of the first occurrence, including that first occurrence itself (`parentEventId === id`). This is the shape `buildGatheringViewModel` already expects and the shape every existing test fixture uses; nothing downstream changes.

**The grouping decision moves out of the creation modal.** The creation path currently decides dates and writes documents in one function inside a form component. The part that matters — given a set of occurrence dates, which documents form one series and which is the anchor — becomes a pure function in the roster/series module, so it is testable without rendering. The modal calls it and writes what it returns.

**The backfill is a one-time script, not a migration hook.** It groups existing Gatherings that carry `isRecurring: true` and no `parentEventId` by name plus weekday, orders each group by date, and stamps every member with the first member's id. Idempotent: a Gathering that already has `parentEventId` is skipped, so a partial run can simply be re-run.

**Grouping by name plus weekday is deliberate, and its limits are accepted.** Two Rhythms that share both a name and a weekday would merge; the team runs none. Two Bible Studies on different weekdays stay separate, which is the case that actually exists. A Rhythm renamed mid-term would split into two series; this is preferable to merging unrelated Gatherings, and is repairable by hand.

**One-offs are left alone.** A Gathering with `isRecurring: false` is untouched by the backfill and continues to render as a one-off.

**No schema change.** `parentEventId` already exists on the type and in the security rules. This issue only makes something write it.

**`attendanceRoster`'s series lookup is not changed.** Its rule (`parentEventId`, falling back to the Gathering's own id when `isRecurring`) starts producing correct results the moment the field is populated. The apply-to-future prompt is fixed by the data, not by new logic.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts what a Full-timer would notice — that a term created through the normal path produces one Rhythm rather than seventeen — not that a particular helper was called or that a document carries a particular key.

**The new pure function carries the logic tests**, in the existing roster module's test file. The cases that matter: a weekly term produces one series anchored at the earliest date; a term whose dates are supplied out of order still anchors at the earliest; a single non-recurring Gathering produces no series; two terms sharing a weekday but not a name stay separate. Prior art: `attendanceRoster.test.ts`, which tests this module in exactly this shape.

**One test must fail before the fix.** A test that builds Gatherings the way the creation path actually writes them — `isRecurring: true`, no `parentEventId` — and asserts a Rhythm row is produced. Today that test fails. This is the regression guard; without it the same defect returns the next time a fixture is hand-written.

**The existing view-model fixtures stay as they are.** They hand-set `parentEventId` and they encode the intended model correctly. They are not wrong; they were simply never joined to a test proving production writes that shape.

**The backfill gets a test over its grouping rule**, not over Firestore: given a list of Gatherings, it returns the id-to-anchor assignments. Running it against the emulator is not required.

**Both existing seams must stay green**: `attendanceRoster.test.ts` and `gatheringViewModel.test.ts`.

## Out of Scope

- **The Gatherings page redesign.** Rhythm as a stored record, retiring the kind taxonomy, the reordered page, the drawer and the two-act create flow are all specced separately. This issue deliberately ships ahead of that work and is not blocked by it.
- **Deleting the anchor Gathering.** Removing the first Gathering of a series orphans the rest, because identity hangs off a real record. Real, still real after this fix, and resolved properly only when a Rhythm becomes its own record.
- **Mobile.** `AttendanceMobile` and the native Gatherings screen share the flat-list problem and are untouched here.
- **Renaming `Event` to `Gathering`.** Cosmetic and bundled with the redesign.

## Further Notes

Vocabulary is in `CONTEXT.md`: a **Gathering** is one occasion attendance is taken for; a **Rhythm** is a Gathering that repeats. The code's `Event` type is the same concept under an older name.

Worth stating plainly for whoever picks this up: the reason this shipped and stayed broken is that every test fixture hand-wrote the field that production never writes. The tests encoded the intended model faithfully and nothing checked the intent against reality. The failing test described above is the point of this issue as much as the fix is.

ADR 0011 notes in passing that a Rhythm is derived rather than stored, citing the anchor lookup. That observation stays true after this fix — this issue populates the derivation, it does not replace it.

title: Security: Full-timers tab posts leak onto trainee mobile home screen (scope:"team" IAM miss)
label: CLOSED
body:
## Summary

Trainees (e.g. Enoch) can see **Full-timers tab** (admin-only) comments about contacts they do not own, appearing as cards on the native mobile home screen.

## Domain context

The **Full-timers tab** on a contact is described in CONTEXT.md as staff-only: _"It is one of the tabs on the contact detail page and is not visible to Trainees."_ Posts there are stored with `scope: "team"` in the shared `contacts/{id}/threads` subcollection.

## Reproduction

1. Full-timer posts a comment/question/nudge in the **Full-timers tab** of any contact.
2. Log in as a Trainee (e.g. Enoch) whose `uid` is not in `createdBy`, `coCreators`, or `owner` for that contact.
3. Open the native mobile app → home screen.
4. **Observed:** A card surfaces the Full-timers tab post (body, author, kind label).
5. **Expected:** No card — the post is admin-only content.

## Root cause: two gaps

### Gap 1 — app layer (fixed in linked PR)

`buildQueue` ([packages/core/src/queue.ts](../blob/main/packages/core/src/queue.ts)) filters full-timer messages by sender uid and `kind` but never checks `scope`. A team-scoped post from any full-timer matched the filter and became a home-screen card.

`traineeWaitingItems` ([packages/core/src/inbox.ts](../blob/main/packages/core/src/inbox.ts)) had the same gap: team-scoped nudges/questions showed up in the "what's waiting on you" list.

The fix mirrors the guard already present in `attention.ts` (line 188):
```ts
// buildQueue — queue.ts
m.scope !== "team" &&

// traineeWaitingItems — inbox.ts
if (m.scope === "team") continue;
```

### Gap 2 — Firestore layer (open, this issue tracks it)

The collection-group `list` rule at `firestore.rules:933`:
```
allow list: if isApprovedUser() && (resource.data.get('scope', '') != 'team' || isAdmin());
```
Firestore **cannot evaluate `resource.data` content in `list` rules for collection-group queries** — the check is silently ignored. The collection-group subscription (`subscribeAllThreads`) therefore returns all thread documents — including `scope: "team"` ones — to any authenticated user.

The nested per-document `allow read` rule (line 271) correctly blocks a single-doc `get`, but the `list` path bypasses it. A Trainee with network capture tooling can observe the raw team-scoped documents in Firestore responses regardless of the app-layer fix.

## Recommended Firestore-layer fix

Either:
- **A.** Move Full-timers tab posts to a separate subcollection `contacts/{id}/adminThreads` with an `isAdmin()`-only read rule (cleanest, requires a data migration and a new collection-group rule).
- **B.** Add a server-side `where('scope', '!=', 'team')` clause to `subscribeAllThreads` when the caller is not an admin (no migration, but couples the query to role).

Option A is the correct long-term fix. Option B is an interim measure.

## What was tested

- Two new regression tests locked the app-layer fix in place (see linked PR).
- All 736 `@cisa/core` unit tests pass.
- The Firestore-layer gap is **not** covered by the existing emulator test suite — a rules test should be added.
