title: Bible study: a Section reads as a card on ground, and the student sets the type size
label: CLOSED
body:
## Problem Statement

A short Section reads as a small thing marooned on a large screen.

The reader top-aligns a Section's content, which was meant to fix the previous arrangement where a short Section floated in the vertical middle with dead space above and below it. It did not fix it — it moved all of the dead space to the bottom. Most Sections in a real week are short: a point, a Passage, a Prompt. So most panels are a cluster of text clinging to the header with an empty band beneath, and the text itself feels undersized against all that emptiness.

The type is genuinely small as well, and the editor preview has been hiding it. Body text renders one step larger on desktop than on a phone, so a Full-timer approving a week has been judging the generous version of it. A student in the back row of a gathering, holding a phone, gets the smaller one, and has no way to ask for anything bigger.

In light mode there is a second problem waiting: the app's light theme fills cards with a grey on a white ground and sets no shadow, so any card treatment applied naively comes out *darker* than what it sits on and reads as a recess rather than an object.

## Solution

The empty space gets a job, and the reader gets a say in the type.

A Section's content sits on a raised card, and the panel around it becomes ground. The space that used to read as a void reads as margin around an object — the same amount of emptiness, doing something. While the content fits, it settles optically in the panel, framed above by air and below by the peek. When a Section is longer than the screen the card simply grows: it stays one continuous surface that runs past the fold and closes below the last block, and the reader scrolls it like anything else.

Body text is set larger by default, and a student can change it. The control lives in the reader and is remembered on that student's device, so the person who cannot read it is the person who can fix it — no author involvement, and nothing stored on the Meeting.

The card reads as an object in both themes, using the physics each theme actually has: in light it catches more light than its ground and carries a layered shadow; in dark it stays lighter than its ground with an edge, because a shadow on near-black is invisible. This is a deliberate local departure from the app's flat light-mode cards, scoped to the reader — a page most of whose audience arrives by scanning a QR at a gathering and never opens the app.

## User Stories

1. As a student reading a short Section, I want its content to sit as a composed object rather than clinging to the top of the screen, so that it does not feel like an offcut.
2. As a student, I want the empty part of a panel to read as deliberate margin, so that the page looks composed rather than unfinished.
3. As a student, I want a short Section to settle optically in the panel, so that my eye lands on the content rather than hunting above it.
4. As a student, I want a Section longer than the screen to keep its card and simply scroll, so that long and short Sections feel like the same kind of thing.
5. As a student, I want a long Section's card to close below its last block, so that I can tell I have reached the end of the Section.
6. As a student, I want the peek to stay at the bottom of the panel under the card, so that I still know what is coming.
7. As a student, I want the card to look raised in light mode, so that it reads as an object and not a grey patch.
8. As a student, I want the card to look raised in dark mode, so that both themes read the same way even though they get there differently.
9. As a student, I want body text large enough to read at arm's length in a room, so that I am not squinting while a leader talks.
10. As a student with poor eyesight, I want to make the text larger, so that I can take part without borrowing someone else's phone.
11. As a student, I want my text size remembered next time I scan, so that I set it once.
12. As a student, I want my text size to be mine, so that changing it does not change what anyone else sees.
13. As a student who has made the text large, I want a Section that no longer fits to scroll normally, so that a bigger size never costs me content.
14. As a student, I want prompts and passages to scale with the body text, so that the page stays in proportion at any size.
15. As a Full-timer, I want the preview to show the same type size a phone shows, so that I stop approving a more generous version of the week than the room gets.
16. As a Full-timer, I want the preview to show the card treatment, so that I am judging the real reading experience.
17. As a Full-timer, I want none of this to require anything of me while writing, so that the reading experience is not another thing to configure per week.
18. As a Full-timer, I want the Meeting to store only the week's text, so that a presentation setting never becomes part of the document.
19. As a future maintainer, I want the reason top-align was replaced written down, so that the change reads as a decision rather than a reversal.
20. As a future maintainer, I want the reader's departure from the app's light-mode card convention recorded, so that nobody "fixes" it back into consistency.

## Implementation Decisions

**A Section's content sits on a card; the panel is ground.** The card carries a radius, generous internal padding and elevation. The peek stays outside the card, at the bottom of the panel, so the trailing space is bounded by something meaningful at both ends.

**Content settles while it fits.** When a Section's content plus its peek is shorter than the panel, the content is pushed off the top edge so it rests optically in the panel. When it does not fit, it top-aligns and overflows normally. This is a continuous behaviour — as content grows the settling offset shrinks to zero — so nothing jumps at the threshold. This amends **ADR 0014 §5**, which removed vertical centring: that decision correctly identified dead space as the problem but treated centring as the cause, and top-aligning only relocated the dead space. Top-align is recorded as the rejected branch.

**An overflowing Section keeps its card.** The card grows into one continuous surface rather than degrading to plain text. The alternative — dropping the card when content does not fit — was considered and rejected on two grounds: it is discontinuous, so a Section one line either side of the threshold looks entirely different and can flip on a rotation or a type change; and combined with the reader-side type control it would hand the plainest treatment to the readers who chose the largest type, which is backwards. The cost is accepted and stated: mid-scroll through a long card no edges are visible, so the object reading weakens exactly when a Section is long.

**Body type defaults larger, and the reader controls it.** The default rises from the current phone size. A control in the reader's chrome offers a small range of sizes and persists the choice in that student's browser storage. Deliberately **not** a Meeting field: `md` is the single source of truth for a Meeting and holds the week's text, not its presentation (ADR 0012, ADR 0013 §5); an author cannot know a reader's eyesight or phone in any case. Prompt and title sizes derive from the body size so the page stays in proportion. This depends on the viewport-keyed size pairs being collapsed first, specified separately.

**The card's internal inset stays constant across sizes.** Scaling the inset down at larger type was considered — the card's side padding costs reading width exactly when the type is largest — and is deliberately deferred rather than shipped. Revisit if the measure proves uncomfortable at the top of the range.

**Light and dark elevate by different means.** The app's light theme fills cards with the panel tone on a white ground and sets no card shadow, which would render the Section card darker than its ground. For the reader the pair is swapped — the panel ground takes the panel tone, the card takes the background tone — and light elevation comes from a layered shadow, while dark keeps elevating through lightness plus an edge because shadow is invisible on near-black. No new colours are introduced; both themes use tokens the app already ships. This changes the reader's light background from white to the panel tone. Scoped to the reader's Section card: every other light-mode card in the app stays flat, and the app-wide card shadow token is not touched.

**Blanks, prompts and passages keep their existing treatments** inside the card, with prompt surfaces reading as insets within it rather than as further raised objects.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts what a student can observe and control: that the reader offers a text-size control, that choosing a size persists and is applied on return, that content still renders correctly at every size. Almost everything else in this change is layout physics, and jsdom has no layout — a test asserting the settling offset, the card's elevation or whether content fits would pass against any implementation, including a broken one. Those are verified in a browser and on a device, and the automated tests cover the state that survives a reload.

**Seam — `StudyReaderView`,** the existing component seam. No new seam is introduced. Cases: the text-size control is present and offers the expected sizes; choosing a size records it in browser storage; a reader mounted with a stored size applies it; a reader with no stored size applies the default; every Section still renders its blocks at every size; the peek and end-of-Meeting treatments still render.

**Seam — `SectionBody`,** existing. Block rendering is unchanged; the suite standing green is the evidence that the type scale is applied without altering what is rendered.

**Seam — `BibleStudyEditor`,** existing. The preview renders the reader including the card treatment; regression only.

**Prior art.** The reader's Blank reveal state and the editor's dismissed-card persistence are the precedents for per-user browser-storage state that must degrade quietly when storage is unavailable — a stored size that cannot be read falls back to the default rather than erroring.

**Not covered by any automated seam.** Settling, card elevation, the light-mode ground swap, and how a long card reads mid-scroll. Verification is browser-preview inspection at emulated phone sizes in both themes, plus a pass on a real iPhone against the QA deploy before merge, covering a short Section, a Section that overflows only at the largest type, and a Section that overflows at every size.

## Out of Scope

- The reader's snapping and read model, the preview's geometry, the toolbar caret jump, and the new toolbar items — all specified separately. This issue assumes the panel geometry fix has landed.
- **Scaling the card's inset with the type size.** Deferred, as above.
- **Haptic feedback on Section change.** Deferred until the fixed snapping can be judged on a device.
- Changing the app-wide light-mode card convention. The reader's departure is local and deliberate; retheming every card in the app is a separate decision with its own audience.
- An author-side type setting, or any new field on the Meeting.
- A theme toggle in the reader. Students get their device's theme; the dark/light toggle in the editor preview is an authoring tool and is unchanged.
- Present mode, the QR, the Weeks index, publishing and the Firestore rules.

## Further Notes

- ADR 0014 §5 needs amending, and the amendment should say plainly that the dead space was the problem and centring was not the cause — otherwise the next person to read §5 and the shipped code will assume one of them is a mistake.
- The reader is treated as its own design surface, free to depart from app-wide conventions, because most people who see it arrive by scanning an Entry point QR at a gathering and never open the tracker. That reasoning is what justifies the light-mode departure and should travel with it.
- The type-size default and the card treatment were chosen from a live comparison of four alternatives at true phone dimensions, in both themes, with a Section that overflows only at the largest sizes. The rejected alternatives were plain top-align, settle without a card, and card without settling.
- Raising the default type makes overflow substantially more common: Sections that fit today will not fit at the new default, and more still will overflow for a student who increases the size. That is expected and is why the overflow behaviour was settled before the default was raised.

title: Bible study: Verse and Apply join the toolbar, Passage loses its placeholder reference, and block inserters land in the caret's Section
label: CLOSED
body:
## Problem Statement

A Full-timer writing a week cannot say two things the studies actually contain, and the toolbar puts the things it can say in the wrong place.

There is only one way to put scripture on a page: a Passage, which sets the words large with the citation trailing underneath in small caps. That is right for a text the room dwells on. It is wrong for a proof-text glanced at mid-thought — the kind written "Rom. 5:6 — while we were still weak…", where the reference leads because the reference is the point. Authors writing those get a pulled-out quotation whether they want one or not.

There is no way to mark an application. Prompts come in three kinds — Question, Discuss, Activity — and the move a study makes at the end, where the room names what they will actually do, has no marker. Reported from the field as "need an apply in bible study editor" (#905).

The Passage button inserts a two-line template with a placeholder reference the author usually has to delete, even though a Passage with no citation is perfectly valid and already renders correctly.

And every block-inserting toolbar button writes at the caret, which means it splits whatever line the author is in the middle of and adds inconsistent blank lines around itself — sometimes running the new block into the previous paragraph, sometimes leaving a gap.

## Solution

The toolbar gains the two things the studies need and stops fighting the author about placement.

**Verse** is a new block: the reference leads, the words follow at body size, and it sits in the flow of the Section rather than pulling out of it. A Passage stays what it is — the text foregrounded, the citation subordinate and trailing. Two different moves, two different blocks, so an author picks the reading they want rather than getting the only one on offer.

**Apply** joins Question, Discuss and Activity as a fourth kind of Prompt, in its own colour, for the part of a Section that asks the room to take something away.

**Passage** inserts a bare quote with no reference line. A citation is added by typing one, the way a Section's name is typed after "+ Add section" — the toolbar stops inserting text the author has to delete.

**Block inserters land at the end of the Section the author is working in,** separated from what came before by exactly one blank line. No split lines, no stray gaps, and the new block lands where the author is writing rather than wherever the cursor happened to be left.

## User Stories

1. As a Full-timer, I want a Verse block where the reference leads and the text follows, so that I can cite a proof-text without it becoming a pulled-out quotation.
2. As a Full-timer, I want a Verse to sit at body size in the flow of the Section, so that it reads as part of the argument rather than an interruption to it.
3. As a Full-timer, I want a Passage to keep setting the words large with the citation trailing, so that the text the room dwells on still gets the weight.
4. As a Full-timer, I want the toolbar to offer Verse and Passage separately, so that I choose the reading rather than discovering it after publishing.
5. As a student, I want a Verse to read as a citation and a Passage to read as a quotation, so that I can tell at a glance which one the leader means to sit with.
6. As a Full-timer, I want an Apply prompt, so that the part of the study where the room names what they will do is marked like the other prompts.
7. As a Full-timer, I want Apply to have its own colour, so that I can pick prompts apart while scanning a week.
8. As a student, I want an Apply prompt to look like a prompt, so that I know it is being put to the room rather than read at me.
9. As a Full-timer, I want the Passage button to insert a bare quote, so that I am not deleting a placeholder reference every time.
10. As a Full-timer, I want to add a citation to a Passage by typing one, so that the reference is optional in practice and not just in principle.
11. As a Full-timer, I want a block-inserting toolbar button to place its block at the end of the Section I am working in, so that it lands where I am writing.
12. As a Full-timer, I want exactly one blank line between the new block and what came before, so that I am not tidying whitespace after every click.
13. As a Full-timer, I want a toolbar click never to split the line I am in the middle of, so that an insertion cannot damage a sentence.
14. As a Full-timer with the caret in the first Section of a six-Section week, I want a Discuss prompt to land in that first Section, so that it does not silently file itself under the last one.
15. As a Full-timer whose caret is not in any Section yet, I want the block to land at the end of the document, so that the behaviour is predictable rather than undefined.
16. As a Full-timer, I want the outline to keep highlighting my Section after an insertion, so that I stay oriented.
17. As a Full-timer, I want the preview to show the new block immediately, so that I can confirm the syntax became what I meant.
18. As a Full-timer, I want inline emphasis and Blanks to keep working inside a Verse, so that the new block is not a second-class citizen.
19. As a Full-timer, I want the same markdown to parse identically in the web app and in the shared core package, so that a week reads the same wherever it is read.
20. As a future maintainer, I want Verse and Apply defined in the project glossary, so that the words mean one thing across code, issues and conversation.

## Implementation Decisions

**Verse is its own block kind, not a display flag on Passage.** The stored data is the same shape either way — some text and a reference — so this was a real choice. It goes to two blocks because the reading is genuinely different and the model should track that: a Passage is a pulled-out quotation, set large with a rule above and the citation subordinate; a Verse is a citation in the flow, at body size, with the reference leading and emphasised. Collapsing them into one block with a presentation flag would put a rendering decision inside a document model whose whole discipline is that a Section reads as the author wrote it. The cost is accepted and stated: a new block kind in both parser mirrors, the parity corpus, the renderer, the toolbar and the glossary.

**Verse needs a marker the grammar can see.** Passage is a blockquote whose last line is the citation; a leading-reference line inside the same construct is not distinguishable from a two-line Passage, so Verse takes its own unambiguous prefix rather than relying on shape detection of a reference. Detecting "looks like a book, chapter and verse" is explicitly rejected: it is fragile, and it would silently reclassify existing Passages whose first line happens to match.

**Apply is a fourth Prompt kind,** joining Question, Discuss and Activity in the prompt-kind union, the prompt line grammar, and the renderer's colour mapping. It takes the ochre tone from the existing palette, which reads warm against the sage, clay and slate already in use without colliding with any of them.

**Both changes land in both parser mirrors and join the parity corpus,** per ADR 0013 §5. Every corpus fixture must produce deep-equal results from both modules; a Full-timer's week must not behave differently depending on which module read it.

**Passage inserts a bare quote.** The reference line is removed from the insertion. The parser already treats a single-line blockquote as a Passage with no citation, so this is an editor-side change only, and it brings the Passage button in line with the principle ADR 0014 §9 already settled for "+ Add section": an inserted thing carries no starter text the author must delete.

**Block inserters append to the end of the caret's Section.** The requested behaviour was the end of the document, and it is not taken, because a Prompt, a Passage and a Verse all live *inside* a Section: appending to the document end would file them under the last Section while the author writes the second, which is the same class of silent misplacement ADR 0014 §9 fixed for Sections one level up. The end of the caret's Section gives everything the request was after — no cursor guesswork, no split lines, a visible result — without that failure. The existing helpers that report Section offsets and the Section containing a given offset supply the boundary. With the caret outside any Section, the insertion falls back to the end of the document. The editor scrolls to the insertion and leaves the caret ready to type, as "+ Add section" does.

**Whitespace is normalised at insertion.** Exactly one blank line separates the new block from the preceding content, regardless of how the document was terminated. Inline inserters — bold, italic, Blank — are unchanged and continue to wrap at the caret; only block-level items move.

**Glossary changes.** `CONTEXT.md` gains **Verse**. **Passage** currently lists "Verse" among the words to avoid, on the understanding that it was a wrong word for Passage; that entry is amended, and Passage's definition sharpens to say the citation is subordinate and trailing. **Prompt** currently says "one of three kinds" and lists "application" among the words to avoid; it becomes four kinds and "application" is struck.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts what an author writes and what a student then sees: that this markdown produces a Verse and that markdown produces a Passage, that an Apply prompt renders as a prompt with its own label, that clicking Discuss puts a Discuss line at the end of the Section the caret is in. Tests that assert a colour token, a class name, or the internal shape of a block are not that.

**Seam — the pure mirror pair,** the highest seam and where all new grammar goes, covered by the existing suites on both modules. Cases: a Verse line parses to a Verse block with its reference and text separated; a blockquote still parses to a Passage, with the last line as the citation when there is more than one line and no citation when there is one; a Verse prefix inside a Section body does not disturb the surrounding blocks; `apply:` parses to a Prompt of that kind, case-insensitively, alongside the existing three; a line that merely looks like a scripture reference is not reclassified as a Verse; the helper that reports where a block insertion belongs returns the end of the caret's Section, and the end of the document when the caret is in no Section.

**Seam — mirror parity,** existing. The corpus grows fixtures containing Verses, Apply prompts and ref-less Passages, and both modules must agree on all of them.

**Seam — `SectionBody`,** the existing renderer seam. Cases: a Verse renders its reference and its text, distinguishably from a Passage; a Passage with no citation renders without one; an Apply prompt renders with its own label; inline emphasis and Blanks work inside a Verse.

**Seam — `BibleStudyEditor`,** existing. Cases: the toolbar offers Verse and Apply; Passage inserts a quote with no reference line; clicking a block inserter with the caret in an early Section appends to the end of *that* Section, not the document; exactly one blank line precedes the inserted block; inline inserters still wrap at the caret.

No new seam is introduced.

## Out of Scope

- **The inline scripture reference** — a citation inside a line of prose with no quoted text. Deliberately deferred; a token would have to be chosen that does not collide with the Blank syntax, and the case can wait.
- **Moving the Blank tokenizer into the parser mirrors.** The Blank split currently lives in the renderer rather than in either mirror, so it escapes the parity requirement ADR 0013 §5 places on grammar. Noted, not fixed here, and not copied — the Verse grammar goes in the mirrors where it belongs.
- Section reorder and delete controls, still deliberately absent.
- Underline, tables and images, still out of the markdown scope per ADR 0013 §2.
- A clipboard-HTML paste handler, still deferred.
- The reader's snapping, the preview's geometry, the toolbar caret jump, and the card and type-scale work — all specified separately.
- Any change to the stored Meeting shape. Sections stay derived from `md`.

## Further Notes

- Closes #905.
- The glossary collisions are worth noting because they are the useful kind: the model said "Verse" was a wrong word for Passage and "application" a wrong word for Prompt, and both turned out to be real distinctions the model had not yet made. Amending them is the model catching up, not the model being wrong.
- Verse and Passage carrying the same data with different renderings is the strongest argument for collapsing them, and it was weighed and rejected. If a third scripture treatment ever appears, revisit whether these are three blocks or one block with a treatment — but not before.
- The insertion-location decision deliberately departs from the literal request. The requester's stated goal was predictability and clean whitespace, both of which the chosen behaviour delivers; the literal reading would have introduced a new silent-misplacement bug of exactly the kind that prompted the request.

title: Bible study: a toolbar click stops throwing the author back to the top of the document
label: CLOSED
body:
## Problem Statement

Clicking a toolbar button in the Meeting editor throws the author back to the top of the document.

A Full-timer writing partway down a long week clicks Passage — or Blank, or bold, or a Prompt — and the textarea scrolls to the beginning. The insertion itself lands correctly, but the author has lost their place and has to scroll back down and find the sentence they were in the middle of. It happens on every block-inserting button, and it happens every time, which makes the toolbar actively unpleasant to use on any week long enough to need scrolling — exactly the weeks where the toolbar saves the most typing.

Reported from the field as "clicking on toolbar items keep pushing me back to top" (#906).

## Solution

The toolbar stops moving the author.

Clicking a toolbar button inserts its text and leaves the document exactly where it was, with the caret placed where the author would expect to continue typing and the view still showing the passage they were working on. Nothing scrolls except when the insertion itself is off screen, in which case the editor brings the new text into view rather than the top of the document.

## User Stories

1. As a Full-timer writing partway down a week, I want clicking a toolbar button to leave my scroll position alone, so that I do not lose the paragraph I am writing.
2. As a Full-timer, I want the caret to stay where the insertion happened, so that I can keep typing immediately.
3. As a Full-timer, I want the text I had selected to still be selected inside the markers after I click bold, so that emphasis behaves the way it does in every other editor.
4. As a Full-timer, I want this to hold for every toolbar button, so that I do not have to learn which ones are safe.
5. As a Full-timer, I want it to hold whether or not I had clicked into the textarea first, so that the toolbar is usable straight after opening a week.
6. As a Full-timer, I want it to hold while a colleague is editing the same Meeting, so that live collaboration does not reintroduce the jump.
7. As a Full-timer, I want the editor to scroll to the insertion when it happens off screen, so that I can see that the click did something.
8. As a Full-timer, I want the outline to keep highlighting the Section my caret is in after an insertion, so that I stay oriented.
9. As a Full-timer, I want autosave to continue behaving exactly as it does today after a toolbar insertion, so that this fix costs me nothing elsewhere.
10. As a future maintainer, I want the cause recorded rather than a defensive scroll restore bolted on, so that the fix is not mistaken for a workaround.

## Implementation Decisions

**Diagnose before fixing.** The symptom has more than one plausible mechanism and they call for different fixes, so the cause is confirmed in the browser first rather than inferred. The two candidates: the toolbar button takes focus on mousedown, so the textarea is blurred at the moment its value is replaced, and a programmatic value assignment on an unfocused textarea resets its scroll position — the subsequent refocus then restores the caret but not the scroll; or the deferred refocus races the controlled re-render, so the selection is applied against a stale value. The confirmed cause determines which of the decisions below is load-bearing; both are cheap and compatible, and the fix is not considered done until the reported symptom is reproduced and then observed to stop.

**The textarea keeps focus across a toolbar click.** Toolbar buttons suppress the default mousedown behaviour that moves focus, which is the standard arrangement for a formatting toolbar over a text field. The field never blurs, so there is no blurred-value-assignment window and no refocus to sequence.

**Insertion preserves scroll explicitly.** The insertion path captures the textarea's scroll offset before the value changes and restores it after the selection is set, so the fix does not depend on browsers agreeing about when a value assignment resets scroll. Where the insertion is outside the visible range, the editor scrolls to the caret rather than leaving it off screen — the author must be able to see that the click did something, which is the same principle ADR 0014 §9 settled for "+ Add section".

**Both edit paths are covered.** The editor writes through a single edit path that routes through the replicated document when live collaboration is connected and through local state otherwise. The scroll and focus handling live on that shared path, so the behaviour is identical whether or not a second Full-timer is in the document.

**Selection semantics are unchanged.** Wrapping markers still leave the previously selected text selected between them; a collapsed caret still lands between the markers. This issue changes where the view is, not where the caret is.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts what the author can observe about the caret and the document. Scroll position itself is not observable in jsdom — it has no layout, so a textarea's scroll offset is always zero and a test asserting it would pass against the broken code. That part of the fix is verified in a browser, and the automated tests cover the caret and content behaviour that must not regress while the scroll handling is added.

**Seam — `BibleStudyEditor`,** the existing view seam with the data layer and `AuthProvider` mocked. No new seam is introduced. Cases: clicking a toolbar button inserts its markers at the caret; a selection is preserved between wrapping markers; the caret lands between the markers when nothing was selected; the textarea still holds focus after a toolbar click; the outline's highlighted row still reflects the caret's Section after an insertion; autosave is still scheduled by a toolbar insertion.

**Prior art.** The existing editor suite already covers the analogous case for "+ Add section" — that it appends at the end even when the textarea has never been focused, and leaves the caret inside the new heading. These cases follow the same shape.

**Not covered by any automated seam.** The scroll position itself. Verification is reproducing the report in the browser on a week long enough to scroll, clicking each toolbar button, and confirming the view does not move.

## Out of Scope

- Where block-level toolbar items insert, which is changing separately — this issue is about the view jumping, and must hold under either insertion location.
- The new toolbar items (Verse, Apply) and the ref-less Passage insertion, specified separately.
- The editor preview's geometry and caret following, specified separately.
- Any change to autosave cadence or the live collaboration transport.
- The unsaved-changes guard, already retired.

## Further Notes

- Closes #906.
- The report's viewport is 1107x662, which is small enough that a week of any length scrolls — worth reproducing at that size rather than on a large monitor, where the symptom may not appear at all.
- If diagnosis shows the cause is the blurred-value-assignment window, the focus fix alone is sufficient and the explicit scroll capture is belt-and-braces; it is kept anyway, because the editor's value is assigned from two different paths and only one of them is under this component's control.

title: Bible study: the editor preview fits its pane and follows the caret without restarting (#897 fidelity)
label: CLOSED
body:
## Problem Statement

The editor's live preview does not fit its pane, does not show a whole phone, and jumps back to the first Section every time the author moves the caret.

The phone frame is drawn wider than the pane that holds it, so it is clipped on the right and the pane grows a horizontal scrollbar. Inside the frame the picture is smaller than the frame itself: the rounded bezel, the border and the shadow are drawn around a full-size phone while the content is painted shrunken inside it, leaving an empty band along the bottom and empty slivers down both sides. The bezel does not hug the screen it is supposed to be the edge of.

Vertically it is worse. The frame is drawn at a fixed full phone height regardless of how tall the pane is, so on a laptop window most of the phone is below the fold. The pane scrolls to compensate, which means the reader's own sticky header and progress rail scroll out of sight — the two pieces of chrome the preview exists to let you check. The Present mode panel is stranded far below.

Moving the caret rebuilds the preview from scratch. #897 asked for the preview to follow the caret to the Section being written; instead every caret move resets it to the first Section and wipes any Blank the author had tapped open. Proofreading the Section you are writing means scrolling the preview back down after every keystroke that crosses a Section boundary.

## Solution

The preview becomes a phone that fits.

The frame occupies exactly the space its scaled picture occupies, so the bezel hugs the screen with no dead band inside it and nothing overflows the pane. The scale is measured from the pane rather than fixed, so the phone fills whatever room the window actually gives it and stays whole when the window changes.

The pane stops scrolling. The phone gets the height that is genuinely available, the Present mode panel sits below it as a fixed row, and the reader's sticky header and progress rail stay visible where a student would see them — because the only thing scrolling is the reader, inside the phone.

The preview follows the caret without restarting. Moving into a Section scrolls the preview to that Section, smoothly, keeping revealed Blanks revealed and the reader's own state intact. The tracking stays one-way: scrolling the preview to inspect a later Section never moves the author's cursor.

## User Stories

1. As a Full-timer, I want the whole phone visible in the preview pane, so that I can judge a Section without scrolling the pane to see the rest of the screen.
2. As a Full-timer, I want the phone's bezel to hug its screen, so that the frame reads as a device rather than a box with a picture floating in it.
3. As a Full-timer, I want no horizontal scrollbar in the preview pane, so that nothing is hidden off the right edge.
4. As a Full-timer, I want the preview to fill the pane on a large window and shrink to fit on a small one, so that I am not punished for working on a laptop.
5. As a Full-timer, I want the preview to stay whole when I resize the window, so that the frame does not need a reload to be usable again.
6. As a Full-timer, I want the reader's sticky header visible in the preview, so that I can check the Meeting title and counter a student sees.
7. As a Full-timer, I want the progress rail visible in the preview, so that I can check the reader's footer chrome without scrolling the pane.
8. As a Full-timer, I want the Present mode panel to stay reachable without a long scroll, so that grabbing the entry point URL is not a hunt.
9. As a Full-timer, I want scrolling inside the preview to scroll the reader, so that I am testing the student's scroll and not the pane's.
10. As a Full-timer, I want moving my caret into a Section to bring that Section into the preview, so that I am proofreading what I am writing.
11. As a Full-timer, I want that to be a scroll rather than a reset, so that I do not lose my place in the preview every time I type.
12. As a Full-timer, I want a Blank I revealed in the preview to stay revealed while I keep writing, so that I can confirm the reveal and carry on.
13. As a Full-timer, I want to scroll the preview to a later Section without my cursor moving, so that inspecting the end of the week does not interrupt a sentence.
14. As a Full-timer, I want the preview to reflect markdown I have typed but not saved, so that I can see a change before deciding to publish.
15. As a Full-timer, I want the dark and light preview toggle to keep working, so that I can check both themes a student might be in.
16. As a Full-timer, I want the preview to render the same component the public reader renders, so that what I approve is what the room gets.
17. As a future maintainer, I want the reason the frame's layout box is pre-scaled written down at the frame, so that the two-box arrangement is not simplified back into the bug.

## Implementation Decisions

**The frame is a two-box arrangement.** A CSS transform is paint-only: scaling an element changes what is drawn without changing the space it occupies. The frame currently scales a full-size phone inside a wrapper sized to the unscaled phone, so the layout box stays full size while the picture shrinks — which is the empty band inside the bezel, the slivers at the sides, and the overflow past the pane, all from one cause. The outer box is sized to the scaled dimensions and the inner box keeps true phone dimensions and is scaled from its top-left corner, so layout and paint agree. The bezel, border and shadow move to the box that matches the picture. This is what ADR 0014 §11's "CSS-scaled into the pane" always meant; the decision does not change, it starts being obeyed. A brief comment at the frame records why the outer box is pre-multiplied, because the arrangement looks redundant to anyone who does not know that transforms do not affect layout.

**The scale is measured, not fixed.** The current scale is a constant chosen to squeak inside a particular pane width, and it fits no pane correctly, including that one. A `ResizeObserver` on the pane drives the scale from the smaller of the width and height ratios against true phone dimensions, so the phone is always whole and always as large as the room allows. A lower bound keeps it legible on very small panes.

**The pane stops being a scroller.** The preview pane becomes a fixed-height column: the phone takes the available height, the Present mode panel is a row beneath it. Nested scrolling is removed — the only scroller in the preview is the reader's own deck, which is the thing under test.

**Caret following is a scroll, not a remount.** The preview is currently keyed on the caret's Section index, so React discards and rebuilds the reader on every change: a fresh reducer starting at the first Section, a fresh scroll container at the top, and an empty Blank map. That is why the preview jumps to Section 1 rather than to the caret's Section, and why revealed Blanks vanish. The key is removed. The reader accepts the Section the preview should be showing and scrolls to that panel when it changes, reusing the same scroll-to path the Section index already uses. Reader state — scroll position, revealed Blanks — persists across edits. Tracking remains strictly one-way: nothing in the reader writes back to the editor's selection.

**The dark/light preview toggle is retained** and continues to theme the frame independently of the app's own theme.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts what a Full-timer can observe — that text typed and not saved appears in the preview, that the preview shows the Section the caret is in, that scrolling the preview leaves the textarea's selection alone. Pixel geometry is not assertable in jsdom, which has no layout, and a test that asserted the scale factor or the frame's computed size would be asserting the implementation rather than the behaviour, and would have passed against the current broken frame.

**Seam — `BibleStudyEditor`,** the existing view seam with the data layer and `AuthProvider` mocked. No new seam is introduced. Cases: the preview renders markdown typed into the textarea but never saved; moving the caret into a later Section asks the browser to scroll that Section's panel into view; the reader is not remounted across a caret move, asserted through observable state rather than render counts — a Blank revealed in the preview stays revealed after an edit elsewhere in the document; scrolling the preview does not change the textarea's selection; the dark/light toggle switches the frame's theme.

**Seam — `StudyReaderView`,** existing. Unchanged by this issue; the suite standing green is the evidence that extracting the followed-Section input did not alter what the reader renders.

**Not covered by any automated seam.** The fit-to-pane scale, the absence of overflow, the bezel hugging its screen, and the pane no longer scrolling are all layout facts, and jsdom has no layout. Verification is browser-preview inspection of the editor at a laptop-sized window and at a large one, confirming the phone is whole in both and that neither axis of the pane scrolls.

## Out of Scope

- The reader's own snapping, read model and panel geometry, specified separately — this issue changes how the preview is framed, not what the reader does inside it.
- The toolbar caret jump reported in #906, specified separately.
- Card treatment, alignment and the reader-side type control, specified separately.
- Editing a Meeting on a phone. The editor stays desktop-only and the preview pane stays hidden below the `lg` breakpoint.
- Present mode, the QR, the Weeks index, publishing and the Firestore rules.
- Any change to the stored Meeting shape. `md` remains the single source of truth.

## Further Notes

- This issue exists because #897's acceptance criteria were not met by the code that closed it: the preview is not scaled to fit the pane, and moving the caret does not scroll the preview to that Section. The decisions in ADR 0014 §11 were right and need no amendment — the implementation departed from them.
- The design artboard for the editor already encodes the correct two-box arrangement, with an outer box at the scaled dimensions and an inner box at true phone dimensions scaled from its top-left corner. The shipped code collapsed it to one box. The artboard's own scale factor is an artboard-scale artifact and is not the number to copy; the technique is.
- The empty band inside the bezel is roughly an eighth of the frame's height, which is why the preview reads as a phone with a large blank footer rather than as a mis-scaled frame. The symptom does not obviously point at the cause.

title: Bible study: the reader's scroll model is inert — wire the panel refs, size panels to the deck, stop the preview inflating type
label: CLOSED
body:
## Problem Statement

A student scrolling a Meeting cannot tell where they are, and the reader will not come to rest.

The `NN / NN` counter in the sticky header never moves off `01`. The progress rail at the bottom never fills. Opening the Section index and tapping a Section does nothing at all — the overlay closes and the reader stays exactly where it was. Tapping the peek — the dimmed next-Section title that is supposed to be the "more below" affordance — also does nothing. Every navigation affordance the reader offers is inert; the only thing that actually works is dragging the scrollbar.

Scrolling itself fights back. A Section will not settle at the top of the screen: scroll a little past the header and the Section title is cut in half, and the deck rests there rather than snapping to either the Section you left or the one you are heading for. ADR 0014 chose scroll-snapping precisely so that forward, back and overshoot-recovery would come free from the browser, and none of it is free — the reader has to hand-place every Section.

A Full-timer proofreading in the editor preview is also being misled about type size, and in the direction that matters: the preview renders body text one step larger than the phone does, so a week that looks comfortable on the desktop preview is tighter in the student's hand.

## Solution

Scrolling starts telling the truth about itself.

Sections come to rest. A Section is sized to the area a student actually reads it in, so every resting position the browser is asked to snap to is a position it can reach. Scroll a little and the deck settles cleanly on a Section boundary with the title where it belongs, rather than parking mid-Section with the heading clipped.

The counter, the progress rail and the Section index highlight all follow the scroll. Whichever Section is on screen is the one the header counts, the one the rail has filled to, and the one the index shows as current — moving forward and back alike.

The Section index and the peek navigate. Tapping a Section in the index scrolls the deck to that Section; tapping the peek goes to the next one. Both are smooth scrolls to a real place, not state changes with nothing behind them.

The reader and the preview agree about type size. Body text, prompts and Section titles are set from the reading surface itself rather than from whatever window the surface happens to be inside, so what a Full-timer approves in the preview is the size the room gets.

## User Stories

1. As a student scrolling a Meeting, I want a Section to come to rest with its title fully visible, so that I am not reading a heading with its top sliced off.
2. As a student, I want the deck to settle on a Section rather than between two of them, so that scrolling feels like moving through a document rather than dragging a map.
3. As a student who overshoots a Section, I want a small scroll back to return me to it cleanly, so that recovering from a flick is not fiddly.
4. As a student, I want the `NN / NN` counter to show the Section I am actually looking at, so that I can tell a leader where I am.
5. As a student, I want the counter to go back down when I scroll back up, so that it is a position indicator and not a high-water mark.
6. As a student, I want the progress rail to fill as I move through the Meeting, so that I can see how much is left without opening anything.
7. As a student, I want the progress rail to unfill when I scroll back, so that it reflects where I am rather than the furthest I ever got.
8. As a student arriving late, I want to open the Section index and tap a Section, so that I can catch up to where the room is.
9. As a student, I want the index to scroll me to the Section I tapped, so that tapping a named place actually takes me there.
10. As a student, I want the index to highlight the Section I am currently in, so that I can orient before choosing where to jump.
11. As a student, I want to tap the peek at the bottom of a Section, so that I can move on without a long drag.
12. As a student on a Section longer than my screen, I want to scroll through all of it normally, so that the page does not fight me at every boundary.
13. As a student on a long Section, I want the deck to snap only at the Section boundary, so that snapping never traps me part-way through a passage I am still reading.
14. As a student on a short Section, I want the whole Section to be reachable without the snap pulling me away, so that I can sit on it while the room discusses.
15. As a Full-timer proofreading in the preview, I want body text at the size a phone renders it, so that I am judging what the student sees.
16. As a Full-timer, I want prompts and Section titles at phone size in the preview too, so that no part of the page is quietly more generous than reality.
17. As a Full-timer, I want the preview's counter and rail to move as I scroll it, so that I can confirm the reader's chrome works before publishing.
18. As a future maintainer, I want the read model to be derived from the scroll rather than owned separately, so that the counter and the rail cannot drift out of agreement with the page.

## Implementation Decisions

**A Section panel is sized to the deck, not to the viewport.** The reader's chrome — the sticky header and the sticky progress rail — are flex siblings of the scroll container, so the container is meaningfully shorter than the browser viewport. Panels were sized against the viewport, which made every panel taller than the box it snaps inside and put every `start` snap position out of reach. Panels are sized to the scroll container instead. `min-height` semantics are kept so a Section longer than the deck still overflows and scrolls normally, and proximity snapping is retained for exactly the reason ADR 0014 §1 gives — mandatory snapping can skip or trap on a Section taller than the viewport. This amends ADR 0014 §1's stated panel height.

**The panel refs are actually wired.** The reader keeps an array of panel elements to observe and to scroll to. That array is currently never populated: the panel is rendered by a component that accepts no ref and is given none, so the array is empty at every read. Two features depend on it and both are dead as a result — the `IntersectionObserver` is never constructed because the observe loop finds nothing to observe, and `jump`'s `scrollIntoView` is called on `undefined`. The panel component takes a ref and the call site supplies one.

**The read model is re-derived, not compared against a stale snapshot.** The observer callback currently guards its dispatch against the section index captured when the observer was built. Because the observer is rebuilt only when the Section count changes, that captured value stays at its initial value for the life of the Meeting, so scrolling back to the first Section can never re-register. The guard reads current state rather than a closed-over copy; the observer's own subscription lifecycle stays keyed to the Section count so it is not torn down and rebuilt on every scroll tick.

**Type size is set from the reading surface, not the browser viewport.** `SectionBody` and the panel title currently set two sizes per element and select between them with a viewport-width breakpoint. Inside the editor preview that breakpoint reads the desktop window, not the 390px frame, so the preview always renders the larger of each pair. The breakpoint-selected pairs are replaced with a single size per element, driven by the reader's own type scale. This is a prerequisite for the reader-side type control specified separately.

**Blank reveal state and scroll position survive.** Nothing in this change remounts the reader; the observer is a subscription over stable elements.

## Testing Decisions

A good test here asserts what a student can observe — that a Section's panel exists and is reachable, that the counter names the Section on screen, that tapping an index row asks the browser to scroll to that Section. Tests that assert a class name, a reducer's internal shape, the existence of an observer, or a render count are not that, and would lock in the very implementation this change is replacing.

**Seam — `StudyReaderView`,** the existing component seam. No new seam is introduced. Cases: one panel per Section is rendered; tapping an index row calls `scrollIntoView` on the panel for that Section (jsdom stubs `scrollIntoView`, and the assertion is that the correct panel was asked, not that the browser moved); tapping a peek does the same for the following Section; the end-of-Meeting treatment appears only on the last panel; the counter renders the Section count.

**Seam — `PublicStudyReader`,** existing. The Entry point → Study → newest published Meeting resolution cases, the never-published and no-active-study states, the permalink fallback and the stale-week chip are regression only and must keep passing untouched.

**Seam — `SectionBody`,** existing. Block rendering and Blank extraction are unchanged; the suite standing green is the evidence that collapsing the type-size pairs changed only size.

**Seam — `BibleStudyEditor`,** existing. The preview renders unsaved markdown; unchanged by this issue and asserted as regression.

**Not covered by any automated seam.** The `IntersectionObserver` read model, scroll-snap resting behaviour, `dvh` and safe-area insets produce no observable result in jsdom, which has no layout and stubs the observer. Verification is browser-preview inspection at emulated phone sizes plus a pass on a real iPhone against the QA deploy before merge — the same standing requirement ADR 0014 records.

## Out of Scope

- The editor preview's frame geometry and caret following, specified separately.
- The toolbar caret jump reported in #906, specified separately.
- Card treatment, alignment and the reader-side type control, specified separately — this issue only removes the viewport-keyed size pairs that make the preview lie.
- Haptic feedback on Section change. Deferred until the fixed snapping can be felt on a device; revisit only if it still reads as mushy.
- Mandatory scroll snapping. Proximity is retained per ADR 0014 §1.
- Section reorder and delete controls, still deliberately absent.
- Present mode, the QR, the Weeks index, Entry point setup, publishing and the Firestore rules.

## Further Notes

- The dead panel-ref array is the single cause behind three separate reported symptoms — a frozen counter, a frozen rail, and a Section index that does nothing. Worth keeping in the record, because each was plausibly a different bug.
- ADR 0014 §1 needs amending for the panel height. The decision it records — proximity snapping, scroll as the navigation model, the read model mirrored from an observer — is unchanged and correct; only the stated measurement was wrong, and it was wrong in a way that prevented the decision from ever taking effect.
- The viewport-keyed type pairs are a general hazard for any component rendered inside the editor preview's scaled frame: a breakpoint inside that frame reads the desktop window. Any future responsive rule in reader components has the same bug latent in it.

title: Bible study: refresh the design artboards to match the shipped reader and editor
label: CLOSED
body:
## Parent

Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#890

## What to build

The Bible study design artboards are brought back in line with what shipped. They currently depict the tap-to-advance deck and the old editor, so anyone designing against them is designing against a reader that no longer exists.

The reader artboards move to the scrolling deck: stacked Section panels, top-aligned content, the sticky header with its counter and stale-week chip, the next-Section peek, and the end-of-Meeting panel. The editor artboard moves to the document-with-navigating-outline shape: clickable outline rows, the caret-highlighted row, the single end-appending add action, the toolbar without a Section button, and the scaled real-reader preview. Retired affordances — the back chevron, the tap-anywhere hint, distraction-free mode — come out.

The Settled table in the Bible study design README is checked against what shipped: its Structure row ("Sections, one per screen; order as written") still holds, because a snap panel is still one Section per screen. Any row this work reversed is edited in place with a pointer to ADR 0014, following the convention ADR 0011 established.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The reader artboards show the scrolling deck: snap panels, top-aligned content, sticky header with stale-week chip, peek, end-of-Meeting panel
- [ ] No artboard depicts tap-to-advance, the back chevron, or distraction-free mode
- [ ] The editor artboard shows the navigating outline, the end-appending add action, the toolbar without a Section button, and the scaled real-reader preview
- [ ] Any Settled row this work reversed is edited in place and points at ADR 0014
- [ ] The Structure row is confirmed still accurate rather than silently left alone

title: Bible study: the editor preview becomes the real reader, scaled to a real phone
label: CLOSED
body:
## Parent

Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#890

## What to build

The editor's live preview becomes the actual reader, so what a Full-timer approves is what the room gets.

Today the preview is a hand-built 320x520 frame with no scrolling, while the Section renderer sets type in fixed pixels sized for a 390-wide phone. Same type, smaller box, no scroll: the preview shows *less* than a real phone shows and crops what it cannot fit, which is the opposite of its job. Its Blanks are stubbed inert, so an author cannot tell whether `[[grace]]` became a tap target or literal brackets.

The preview now renders the shared reader component over the author's unsaved markdown, at true phone dimensions, CSS-scaled to fit the pane. It is the real reading surface: the sticky header, the snap panels, the peek, the working Blanks.

It follows the author. The Section containing the caret is the Section the preview scrolls to, so proofreading tracks writing without hunting. The tracking is one-way: scrolling the preview moves only the preview, never the caret, because a scroll yanking the cursor mid-sentence is hostile.

The dark/light toggle is kept.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The preview renders the same component the public reader route renders
- [ ] The preview reflects markdown that has been typed but not saved
- [ ] The preview renders at true phone dimensions and is scaled to fit the pane, rather than being drawn at a smaller size
- [ ] The preview scrolls, and shows the sticky header, panels and peek that a student sees
- [ ] Tapping a Blank in the preview reveals its word
- [ ] Moving the caret into a Section scrolls the preview to that Section
- [ ] Scrolling the preview does not move the caret in the markdown editor
- [ ] The dark/light preview toggle still works
- [ ] No new component-level test seam is introduced; the preview is covered through the existing editor view seam

title: Bible study: reader chrome for the scrolling deck — sticky header, stale-week chip, next-Section peek
label: CLOSED
body:
## Parent

Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#890

## What to build

The scrolling reader gets the chrome that suits it, and sheds the chrome that was compensating for the deck.

A slim sticky header carries the Meeting title and the Section counter, and stays put as the student scrolls. The progress rail sticks to the bottom. When the reader has fallen back to an older week, the stale-week date condenses into a chip inside that sticky header rather than a banner that scrolls out of sight — a student who lands on the fourth Section of a three-week-old Meeting still has to be able to see it is old. Falling back is right; falling back silently is not (ADR 0011 §3).

Each panel's trailing space stops being dead air and becomes the **peek**: a dimmed sliver of the next Section's title, which is both the cue that more exists and a preview of what is coming. The final panel shows an end-of-Meeting treatment instead.

Three controls go away, because the model they served is gone: the back chevron (scrolling is back), the "Tap anywhere to go on" hint (the peek says it better), and distraction-free mode — its `unadorned` state and `toggleUnadorned` action leave both `readerReducer` mirrors, since the chrome it dimmed is no longer busy enough to warrant hiding.

Header and footer respect safe-area insets so nothing sits under a notch or a home indicator.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The sticky header shows the Meeting title and Section counter and remains visible while scrolling
- [ ] The progress rail is visible from any scroll position and reflects the current Section
- [ ] On a fallback Meeting, the older week's date is visible from any panel, not only the first
- [ ] Each panel shows a dimmed sliver of the next Section's title in its trailing space
- [ ] The last panel shows an end-of-Meeting treatment instead of a peek
- [ ] The back chevron and the "Tap anywhere to go on" hint no longer exist
- [ ] Distraction-free mode is gone: no control, and `unadorned`/`toggleUnadorned` removed from both `readerReducer` mirrors
- [ ] Header and footer clear the safe-area insets
- [ ] The Section index remains reachable and still jumps

title: Bible study: adding a Section is visible — one end-appending action, no toolbar twin
label: CLOSED
body:
## Parent

Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#890

## What to build

When a Full-timer adds a Section, they can see that it happened.

Today "+ Add section" inserts at the markdown editor's cursor — which is offset 0 if the editor has never been focused — so the new heading is written silently to the *top* of the document while the author is looking at the bottom, the outline does not scroll to it, and the selected Section does not change. The author clicks a button, the document looks unchanged, and reasonably concludes nothing happened. A second button in the toolbar does the same thing from a second place, equally invisibly.

Now there is exactly one way to add a Section. "+ Add section" appends a new heading at the **end** of the document regardless of where the cursor is or whether the editor has ever been focused, scrolls there, and leaves the caret after the hashes so the author immediately types the name and watches the outline row appear as they type. The toolbar's Section button is removed; the toolbar becomes only things that go *inside* a Section — Passage, Blank, bold, italic, Question, Discuss, Activity.

A new Section carries no starter body. The editor's placeholder teaches the three moves — a point, a `>` Passage, a marked Prompt — without inserting text the author has to delete.

A `##` typed in the middle of a Section body genuinely splits that Section, because Sections are derived from the markdown. The outline updates live and the split is surfaced quietly rather than happening silently; silent structural change is the class of bug this ticket exists to end.

The append logic goes into the pure `bibleStudy` mirror pair as a function returning the new markdown and the caret offset, so the behaviour is testable without a DOM. Both mirrors stay in step and must agree across the parity corpus.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] "+ Add section" appends at the end of the document even when the markdown editor has never been focused
- [ ] After adding, the editor scrolls to the new heading and the caret sits inside it, ready to type the title
- [ ] The new Section's outline row appears and updates live as the title is typed
- [ ] A newly added Section has an empty body; the guidance is placeholder text, not inserted content
- [ ] The toolbar no longer offers a Section button, and still offers Passage, Blank, bold, italic, Question, Discuss and Activity
- [ ] Typing a `##` inside a Section body splits it, the outline updates immediately, and the split is surfaced to the author rather than being silent
- [ ] A pure function returns the appended markdown plus the caret offset, exists in both `bibleStudy` mirrors, and both agree across the parity corpus
- [ ] Publishing, saving and the unsaved-changes guard are unchanged

## Blocked by

- Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#893

title: Bible study: the reader scrolls — Sections become snap panels, tap-to-advance retires
label: CLOSED
body:
## Parent

Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#890

## What to build

A student who scans the Entry point QR can scroll through the Meeting — forward, back, and back again — instead of being able only to tap forward.

Today the reader is a deck: one Section is rendered at a time, tapping anywhere advances, and the only way back is a small chevron in the corner. A student who overshoots, or who wants the Passage the group is still discussing, is stuck. This replaces that model with scrolling.

Every Section renders as its own panel, stacked vertically, each at least the height of the viewport, with scroll snapping at panel boundaries. Snapping is *proximity*, not mandatory: a Section longer than the screen scrolls normally and only snaps at its edge, which is the case mandatory snapping traps people in. Section content top-aligns within its panel rather than floating in the vertical middle, so the title lands at the same height every time and the eye has one place to look.

Scroll position becomes the single owner of "which Section am I on". The component observes which panel is visible and mirrors that into state as a read model for the counter, the progress rail and the index highlight — state never drives scroll. The Section index still jumps, by scrolling rather than by dispatching.

Tap-to-advance is removed entirely. Blanks keep their taps and stop having to defend themselves against the surrounding click target.

Viewport sizing moves off `vh`, which on mobile Safari makes the card taller than the visible area and hides the bottom chrome under the browser toolbar.

Both `readerReducer` mirrors lose their `advance` and `back` actions; the web app's and `@cisa/core`'s copies must stay in step. jsdom implements neither `IntersectionObserver` nor `scrollIntoView`, so both get stubs in the shared test setup alongside the `matchMedia` stub already there.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every Section of the Meeting renders as its own panel, not just the current one
- [ ] Scrolling moves between Sections in both directions, and a Section taller than the viewport scrolls through normally before snapping
- [ ] Panels come to rest filling the viewport, sized in `dvh` so the full card fits inside mobile Safari's visible area
- [ ] Section content top-aligns; the title sits at the same height on every panel
- [ ] Tapping the body does not change the visible Section
- [ ] Tapping a Blank still reveals it, and a revealed Blank stays revealed when scrolled away from and back
- [ ] The counter, progress rail and index highlight reflect the panel actually on screen after a scroll
- [ ] The Section index still jumps to a chosen Section
- [ ] `advance` and `back` are gone from both `readerReducer` mirrors; `jump`, `revealBlank`, `openIndex`, `closeIndex` and `setTotalSections` still behave
- [ ] `IntersectionObserver` and `scrollIntoView` stubs live in the shared test setup
- [ ] `Section.long` is checked for remaining consumers and deleted from both mirrors if it has none
- [ ] The reader's resolution states (nothing published, never published, no active Study, stale-week fallback) still behave

## Blocked by

- Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#892

title: Bible study: the editor's Section outline navigates the week
label: CLOSED
body:
## Parent

Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#890

## What to build

A Full-timer writing a week can navigate it from the outline. The left pane already lists the `##` headings but is inert, so a long Meeting has to be navigated by scrolling and squinting.

Clicking an outline row now focuses the markdown editor, places the caret at that Section's heading, and scrolls it into view. The row containing the caret is highlighted, so the author always knows which Section they are in. This is navigation and never mutation: clicking a row changes where you are, never what the document says.

Sections remain derived from `md` — no storage change, no per-Section documents.

The load-bearing logic goes into the pure `bibleStudy` mirror pair rather than the component: a function giving the character offset of each Section heading, and a function mapping a caret offset to the Section it falls in. Both mirrors (the web app's and `@cisa/core`'s) must stay in step under the existing keep-in-step rule, and both must agree across the shared parity corpus.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The outline lists every `##` heading in the document, live as it is typed
- [ ] Clicking an outline row moves the editor's caret to that heading and scrolls it into view
- [ ] The outline row containing the caret is visibly highlighted, and follows the caret as the author types or clicks around
- [ ] A pure function returns each Section heading's character offset; a headingless document returns no offsets
- [ ] A pure function maps a caret offset to its Section index, covering offset 0 in a document opening with prose, an offset exactly on a heading, and an offset past the last heading
- [ ] Both functions exist in both `bibleStudy` mirrors and produce deep-equal results across the mirror parity corpus
- [ ] The editor's existing behaviour (save, publish, toolbar inserters, unsaved-changes guard) is unchanged

title: Bible study: extract the shared reader component from the public reader route
label: CLOSED
body:
## Parent

Shir0o/cisa-campus-work-tracker#890

## What to build

A prefactor with no user-visible change: the public reader's presentational half becomes its own component that takes a Meeting as a prop and renders it, while the route keeps everything about *resolving* which Meeting to show.

Today one component does both jobs — it subscribes to the Entry point, the Study and the published Meetings, runs `resolveScan`, renders the three empty states (nothing published, never published, no active Study), and also draws the Section, the chrome and the index. Splitting them lets the editor's live preview later render the identical reading surface over unsaved markdown instead of maintaining a hand-built imitation of it, which is what ADR 0013 §3 asked for and what the current 320x520 mimic frame quietly broke.

Nothing about the reading experience changes in this ticket. The proof is that the existing reader suite passes untouched.

Note on sequencing: the spec (#890) put this extraction last. It is first here because the reader rework then lands *inside* the shared component rather than being moved afterwards. The preview wiring still ships last.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A component exists that renders a Meeting's reading surface from props alone, with no Firestore subscriptions and no knowledge of Entry points or Studies
- [ ] The public reader route still owns the subscriptions, `resolveScan`, the stale-week fallback and all three empty states
- [ ] The existing `PublicStudyReader` test suite passes without modification
- [ ] The shared reader component is not given its own test suite — it is exercised through the existing view seams
- [ ] No change to `SectionBody`, the markdown grammar, or either `bibleStudy` mirror
